statement:
A model achieves 99% accuracy on training data but only 62% on test data. Which of the following best describes this situation?
A) Underfitting due to high bias
B) Overfitting due to high variance
C) Good generalization
D) Data leakage
solution: The large gap between training accuracy (99%) and test accuracy (62%) is the classic signature of overfitting (high variance). The model has memorized training examples rather than learning generalizable patterns.
explanation: Bias-variance tradeoff: high variance = model too complex, fits noise in training data. High bias = model too simple, underfits both sets. Here training accuracy is excellent but test accuracy is poor → high variance / overfitting.

statement:
You are training a regression model to predict house prices. Your dataset contains several extreme outliers (houses sold at 10x normal price). Which loss function makes your model most robust to these outliers?
A) Mean Squared Error (MSE)
B) Mean Absolute Error (MAE)
C) Huber Loss
D) Cross-Entropy Loss
solution: MAE uses absolute differences, so a single outlier with error 1000 contributes 1000 to the loss. MSE squares that error, contributing 1,000,000 — amplifying outlier influence dramatically. MAE is more robust. Huber loss is also robust but MAE is the most straightforward robust choice here. Cross-entropy is for classification.
explanation: MSE penalizes large errors quadratically, making it sensitive to outliers. MAE penalizes linearly. When outliers are genuine noise you want to ignore, MAE is preferred.

statement:
A cancer screening model labels 1000 patients. 50 actually have cancer. The model predicts 'cancer' for 10 patients, all of whom truly have cancer. What is the model's recall?
A) 100%
B) 20%
C) 1%
D) 50%
solution: Recall = True Positives / (True Positives + False Negatives). TP = 10 (correctly identified). FN = 50 - 10 = 40 (missed cancer cases). Recall = 10 / (10 + 40) = 10/50 = 0.20 = 20%.
explanation: Despite 100% precision (all predictions correct), the model misses 80% of cancer cases. In medical screening, recall (sensitivity) is critical — missing a cancer patient is very costly.

statement:
You add L2 regularization (Ridge) to a linear regression model. What is the primary effect on the model weights?
A) Some weights are set exactly to zero
B) All weights are shrunk towards zero but rarely reach zero
C) The model becomes non-linear
D) Weights are normalized to sum to 1
solution: L2 regularization adds a penalty λ||w||² to the loss. The gradient of this penalty pushes weights toward zero proportionally to their magnitude, but the squared penalty means weights approach zero asymptotically — they are rarely exactly zero. L1 (Lasso) produces sparse solutions with exact zeros.
explanation: L1 (Lasso) → sparsity (some weights = 0, useful for feature selection). L2 (Ridge) → weight shrinkage toward 0 but not exactly 0. Elastic Net combines both.

statement:
A decision tree is grown without any depth limit on a training set of 1000 samples. What will most likely happen?
A) The tree will underfit the training data
B) The tree will perfectly memorize the training data with 100% training accuracy
C) The tree will have poor training accuracy but good test accuracy
D) The tree cannot be grown without a depth limit
solution: An unconstrained decision tree can create a leaf for every single training example, perfectly memorizing all labels. This leads to 100% training accuracy but very poor generalization (test accuracy). This is extreme overfitting.
explanation: Decision trees are prone to overfitting when unconstrained. Techniques to control this: max_depth, min_samples_split, min_samples_leaf, pruning, or using ensemble methods like Random Forest.

statement:
In a Support Vector Machine (SVM), what is the role of the 'kernel trick'?
A) It reduces the number of support vectors
B) It maps data to a higher-dimensional space to make it linearly separable without computing coordinates explicitly
C) It speeds up training by pruning the dataset
D) It normalizes the input features
solution: The kernel trick computes dot products in a higher-dimensional feature space without explicitly mapping data there. For example, a polynomial kernel k(x,y) = (x·y + 1)^d implicitly works in a high-dimensional space. This allows SVMs to find non-linear decision boundaries efficiently.
explanation: Common kernels: Linear, Polynomial, RBF (Radial Basis Function / Gaussian), Sigmoid. The RBF kernel can map data to infinite-dimensional space.

statement:
Which of the following is a key limitation of the K-Means clustering algorithm?
A) It can only cluster data with numerical features
B) It requires the number of clusters K to be specified in advance
C) It cannot handle datasets with more than 1000 points
D) It always converges to the global optimum
solution: K-Means requires K to be specified before running. Methods like the Elbow Method or Silhouette Score help choose K but it's not automatic. K-Means also converges to local optima (not guaranteed global), and assumes spherical clusters of similar size.
explanation: Other K-Means limitations: sensitive to initialization (mitigated by K-Means++), assumes spherical clusters, sensitive to outliers. DBSCAN and hierarchical clustering don't require K upfront.

statement:
Naive Bayes classifiers assume that all features are:
A) Normally distributed
B) Conditionally independent given the class label
C) Correlated with each other
D) Binary-valued
solution: The 'naive' assumption in Naive Bayes is conditional independence: P(x1,x2,...,xn|y) = P(x1|y)·P(x2|y)·...·P(xn|y). This simplifies computation enormously. Despite being rarely true in practice, Naive Bayes often works well for text classification (spam detection, sentiment analysis).
explanation: Despite the strong independence assumption, Naive Bayes is competitive for text classification. Variants: Gaussian NB (continuous features), Multinomial NB (word counts), Bernoulli NB (binary features).

statement:
You have a dataset of 100 samples and want to perform 5-fold cross-validation. How many samples are used for training in each fold?
A) 20
B) 80
C) 50
D) 100
solution: In 5-fold CV, the data is split into 5 equal parts of 20 samples each. In each fold, 1 part (20 samples) is used for validation and the remaining 4 parts (80 samples) are used for training. This is repeated 5 times, each time using a different fold for validation.
explanation: K-fold CV gives a more reliable estimate of model performance than a single train/test split. Leave-One-Out CV (LOOCV) is the extreme case where K = N.

statement:
In gradient descent, a very large learning rate can cause the optimization to:
A) Converge very slowly
B) Get stuck in local minima
C) Oscillate or diverge, failing to converge
D) Always find the global minimum faster
solution: If the learning rate is too large, gradient descent takes steps that are too big and may overshoot the minimum — bouncing back and forth across it or diverging entirely. If too small, it converges very slowly. The optimal learning rate balances speed and stability.
explanation: Learning rate schedules (decay over time), adaptive methods (Adam, RMSProp, Adagrad), and techniques like learning rate warmup help manage this tradeoff.

statement:
Feature importance in a Random Forest is typically computed by:
A) The coefficient magnitude in a linear model
B) How much each feature decreases impurity (e.g., Gini) on average across all trees
C) The correlation coefficient between feature and target
D) The p-value from a statistical test
solution: Random Forest feature importance (mean decrease impurity) measures the average reduction in Gini impurity (or entropy) contributed by splits on each feature, averaged across all trees in the forest. Features used higher in trees (closer to root) tend to have higher importance as they affect more samples.
explanation: Alternative importance measures: permutation importance (measures accuracy drop when feature values are shuffled), SHAP values (game-theoretic, more principled). MDI can be biased toward high-cardinality features.

statement:
Logistic regression outputs a value between 0 and 1 because it applies which function to the linear combination of inputs?
A) ReLU
B) Softmax
C) Sigmoid
D) Tanh
solution: Logistic regression applies the sigmoid function σ(z) = 1/(1+e^(-z)) to the linear combination z = w·x + b. The sigmoid maps any real number to (0,1), which can be interpreted as a probability. For multi-class, softmax generalizes sigmoid.
explanation: Sigmoid: σ(z) = 1/(1+e^(-z)), output in (0,1). Decision boundary is where σ(z) = 0.5, i.e., z = 0. Despite being called 'regression', logistic regression is a classification algorithm.

statement:
What is the key difference between Bagging and Boosting ensemble methods?
A) Bagging uses decision trees; boosting uses neural networks
B) Bagging trains models in parallel on random subsets; boosting trains models sequentially, each correcting previous errors
C) Bagging reduces bias; boosting reduces variance
D) Bagging only works for classification; boosting only for regression
solution: Bagging (Bootstrap Aggregating): trains multiple models independently in parallel on random bootstrap samples, then aggregates predictions (e.g., majority vote). Reduces variance. Example: Random Forest. Boosting: trains models sequentially, each one focusing on examples the previous model got wrong. Reduces bias. Examples: AdaBoost, Gradient Boosting, XGBoost.
explanation: Random Forest = Bagging + feature randomness. XGBoost/LightGBM = Gradient Boosting with regularization. Boosting often achieves better accuracy but is slower and more prone to overfitting than bagging.

statement:
Principal Component Analysis (PCA) finds components that:
A) Maximize classification accuracy
B) Maximize variance in the projected data
C) Minimize the number of features
D) Maximize correlation with the target variable
solution: PCA finds orthogonal directions (principal components) that maximize the variance of the projected data. The first PC captures the most variance, the second captures the most remaining variance while being orthogonal to the first, and so on. PCA is unsupervised — it doesn't use class labels.
explanation: PCA is an unsupervised technique for dimensionality reduction and visualization. LDA (Linear Discriminant Analysis) is a supervised alternative that maximizes class separability. t-SNE and UMAP are non-linear alternatives for visualization.

statement:
In K-Nearest Neighbors classification, increasing K (number of neighbors) generally:
A) Increases variance and decreases bias
B) Decreases variance and increases bias
C) Has no effect on bias or variance
D) Always improves accuracy
solution: With small K (e.g., K=1), the model is very sensitive to individual points — high variance, low bias, prone to overfitting. With large K, the decision boundary is smoother and more stable — lower variance but higher bias, tending to underfit. K=N would just predict the majority class for everything.
explanation: KNN is a non-parametric lazy learner — it doesn't learn a model, just stores training data. Prediction time is O(N·d) per query. Feature scaling is essential since KNN uses distance measures.

statement:
Your dataset has 95% negative samples and 5% positive samples. A model that always predicts 'negative' achieves 95% accuracy. Which metric best evaluates useful model performance here?
A) Accuracy
B) F1-Score
C) Mean Squared Error
D) R-squared
solution: With imbalanced data, accuracy is misleading (95% just by always predicting majority class). F1-Score = 2·(Precision·Recall)/(Precision+Recall) balances both precision and recall, and is 0 for a model that always predicts negative (since recall=0). Other useful metrics: AUC-ROC, PR-AUC, Matthews Correlation Coefficient.
explanation: For severely imbalanced problems: use SMOTE (synthetic oversampling), class weights, threshold tuning, or undersampling. Always stratify train/test splits to maintain class ratio.

statement:
You tune a model's hyperparameters using grid search with 5-fold cross-validation on your training set, then report the best CV score as your model's performance estimate. Why might this estimate be optimistic?
A) Cross-validation always underestimates model performance
B) The hyperparameters were selected to maximize performance on the same data used to estimate it
C) 5 folds are not enough for any valid estimate
D) Grid search cannot be used with cross-validation
solution: When hyperparameters are tuned to maximize CV score, the CV score itself becomes a biased (optimistic) estimate — you've essentially 'peeked' at the validation data during hyperparameter selection. This is a form of overfitting to the validation set. The correct approach is a held-out test set that is never used during model development, evaluated only once at the very end.
explanation: Correct procedure: Train/Validation/Test split OR nested cross-validation (outer loop estimates generalization, inner loop tunes hyperparameters). Never use the test set for model selection.

statement:
In linear regression, the ordinary least squares (OLS) solution minimizes:
A) The sum of absolute residuals
B) The sum of squared residuals
C) The maximum residual
D) The number of non-zero coefficients
solution: OLS minimizes the sum of squared residuals: Σ(yi - ŷi)². The squared term makes the objective function differentiable and convex, leading to a closed-form solution: w = (X^T X)^(-1) X^T y. This is only possible when X^T X is invertible (no perfect multicollinearity).
explanation: OLS assumptions: linearity, independence, homoscedasticity (constant variance), normality of residuals. When assumptions are violated, alternatives include robust regression (minimizes absolute residuals) or generalized least squares.

statement:
Before training a KNN classifier, why is feature scaling (e.g., standardization) important?
A) KNN requires all features to be binary
B) Features with larger ranges would dominate the distance calculation
C) Scaling improves the training speed of KNN
D) KNN cannot handle continuous features without scaling
solution: KNN classifies based on distance to neighbors. If feature A has range [0, 1000] and feature B has range [0, 1], then distance is almost entirely determined by feature A. Standardization (z-score) or min-max normalization ensures all features contribute equally to distance.
explanation: Distance-based algorithms requiring feature scaling: KNN, SVM (with RBF kernel), K-Means, PCA. Algorithms NOT requiring scaling: Decision Trees, Random Forest, Naive Bayes (distances not used).

statement:
A binary classifier has the following confusion matrix:
- True Positives (TP): 80
- False Positives (FP): 20
- False Negatives (FN): 40
- True Negatives (TN): 860
What is the precision of this classifier?
A) 66.7%
B) 80%
C) 93.5%
D) 85.7%
solution: Precision = TP / (TP + FP) = 80 / (80 + 20) = 80 / 100 = 0.80 = 80%. Precision measures: of all positive predictions, how many were actually positive? Recall = TP / (TP + FN) = 80 / (80 + 40) = 66.7%. Accuracy = (TP + TN) / total = (80 + 860) / 1000 = 94%.
explanation: Precision and recall trade off against each other as you change the classification threshold. F1 = 2·(0.80·0.667)/(0.80+0.667) = 72.7% is the harmonic mean, balancing both.

statement:
The vanishing gradient problem in deep neural networks occurs most severely with which activation function?
A) ReLU
B) Sigmoid
C) Leaky ReLU
D) GELU
solution: The sigmoid function σ(x) has maximum gradient of 0.25 (at x=0). In deep networks, gradients are multiplied layer by layer during backpropagation. If each layer multiplies by ≤0.25, the gradient becomes exponentially small in early layers (0.25^10 ≈ 0.000001), making learning very slow or impossible.
explanation: ReLU solves vanishing gradients for positive inputs (gradient = 1) but introduces 'dying ReLU' (neurons stuck at 0 for negative inputs). Leaky ReLU fixes dying ReLU with a small slope for negative inputs. Batch normalization also helps with vanishing gradients.

statement:
Backpropagation computes gradients using:
A) Forward differences approximation
B) The chain rule of calculus applied recursively from output to input
C) Random sampling of gradient directions
D) Second-order Taylor expansion
solution: Backpropagation applies the chain rule: ∂L/∂wi = ∂L/∂a · ∂a/∂z · ∂z/∂wi, where L is loss, a is activation, z is pre-activation, wi is a weight. Gradients flow backward from the loss through each layer, enabling efficient computation of all weight gradients in O(parameters) time.
explanation: Forward pass: compute activations from input to output. Backward pass: compute gradients from output to input using chain rule. The key insight is reusing intermediate computations — each gradient builds on previously computed gradients.

statement:
In a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), what is the purpose of pooling layers?
A) To add non-linearity to the network
B) To reduce spatial dimensions and provide translation invariance
C) To normalize activations across the batch
D) To connect all neurons to all neurons in the next layer
solution: Pooling layers (Max Pool, Average Pool) reduce the spatial size of feature maps, decreasing computational cost and the number of parameters. Max pooling selects the maximum value in each window, providing some translation invariance — a feature slightly shifted in position produces the same pooled output.
explanation: Max pooling: takes maximum activation in each window. Average pooling: takes average. Global average pooling: reduces each feature map to a single value. Modern architectures (ResNet, etc.) often use strided convolutions instead of explicit pooling.

statement:
Dropout regularization works by:
A) Removing neurons with low activation permanently
B) Randomly setting neuron outputs to zero during training with probability p
C) Adding Gaussian noise to all weights
D) Reducing the learning rate during training
solution: During training, each neuron is independently zeroed out with probability p (dropped). During inference, all neurons are active but outputs are scaled by (1-p) to maintain expected values (or equivalently, training activations are scaled by 1/(1-p)). This prevents co-adaptation of neurons and acts as implicit ensemble learning.
explanation: Dropout forces the network to learn redundant representations — no single neuron can be relied upon too heavily. Common p values: 0.2-0.5. Applied after activation in fully-connected layers, less common in convolutional layers. Batch normalization partially replaces the need for dropout.

statement:
Batch Normalization normalizes activations within a mini-batch and then applies learnable parameters γ (scale) and β (shift). Why are γ and β necessary?
A) To speed up computation
B) To allow the network to undo the normalization if that is optimal for the task
C) To reduce memory usage
D) To prevent gradient explosion only
solution: Without γ and β, all layers would be forced to have zero mean and unit variance, which may not be the ideal representation. γ and β are learnable parameters that allow the network to learn the optimal scale and shift for each feature — potentially recovering the original distribution if needed. This preserves the model's representational capacity.
explanation: Batch norm computes: ẑ = (z - μ_batch)/σ_batch, then outputs γ·ẑ + β. Benefits: faster training, allows higher learning rates, acts as regularizer, reduces sensitivity to initialization. Issue: behavior differs between training and inference (uses running mean/variance at inference time).

statement:
Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) struggle with long sequences primarily because of:
A) High memory requirements for the hidden state
B) Vanishing or exploding gradients during backpropagation through time
C) Inability to process variable-length sequences
D) Slow inference speed
solution: During backpropagation through time (BPTT), gradients are multiplied by the recurrent weight matrix at each time step. If the largest singular value < 1, gradients vanish exponentially over long sequences. If > 1, they explode. This makes it hard to learn long-range dependencies. LSTMs and GRUs address this with gating mechanisms.
explanation: LSTM (Long Short-Term Memory) uses input gate, forget gate, output gate, and cell state to selectively remember/forget information — gradients can flow through the cell state relatively unchanged. GRU is a simpler variant with fewer gates.

statement:
Transfer learning is most beneficial when:
A) You have a very large labeled dataset specific to your task
B) Your task dataset is small but a related large dataset exists with a pre-trained model
C) Your task is completely unrelated to any existing datasets
D) You need to train a model from scratch for maximum accuracy
solution: Transfer learning takes a model pre-trained on a large dataset (e.g., ImageNet for vision, large text corpora for NLP) and fine-tunes it on a smaller task-specific dataset. Early layers learn general features (edges, textures) that transfer well; later layers learn task-specific features. This requires far less data and compute than training from scratch.
explanation: Strategies: feature extraction (freeze pre-trained layers, train only new head), fine-tuning (unfreeze some/all layers with small learning rate), domain adaptation. BERT, GPT, ResNet are common transfer learning bases.

statement:
The Adam optimizer combines which two techniques?
A) L1 and L2 regularization
B) Momentum and RMSProp (adaptive learning rates)
C) Dropout and Batch Normalization
D) Gradient clipping and weight decay
solution: Adam (Adaptive Moment Estimation) maintains: m_t (first moment — exponential moving average of gradients, like momentum) and v_t (second moment — exponential moving average of squared gradients, like RMSProp). The update is: w = w - α · m̂_t / (√v̂_t + ε). Bias correction (m̂, v̂) corrects for initialization near zero.
explanation: Adam hyperparameters: α (learning rate, default 0.001), β1 (momentum decay, default 0.9), β2 (RMS decay, default 0.999), ε (numerical stability, default 1e-8). AdamW fixes weight decay in Adam. Generally a good default optimizer.

statement:
In the Transformer architecture, the self-attention mechanism computes attention scores using:
A) Convolutional filters applied to the sequence
B) Dot products between Query and Key vectors, scaled by √d_k
C) Recurrent connections between time steps
D) Element-wise multiplication of input embeddings
solution: Self-attention: for each position, compute Q (query), K (key), V (value) projections. Attention weights = softmax(QK^T / √d_k). Output = attention_weights · V. The √d_k scaling prevents extremely small gradients when d_k is large (dot products grow with dimension, pushing softmax into saturation region).
explanation: Multi-head attention runs h parallel attention heads, each learning different relationships. Positional encodings (sine/cosine or learned) add position information since attention is permutation-invariant. Complexity: O(n²·d) per layer — quadratic in sequence length n.

statement:
For a multi-class classification problem with 10 classes, which combination of output activation and loss function is standard?
A) Sigmoid + MSE
B) Softmax + Cross-Entropy
C) ReLU + Hinge Loss
D) Tanh + MAE
solution: Softmax converts logits to a probability distribution summing to 1 across all classes. Cross-entropy loss L = -Σ y_i log(p_i) penalizes the model when it assigns low probability to the correct class. Sigmoid is for binary or multi-label classification. MSE is for regression.
explanation: For binary classification: sigmoid + binary cross-entropy. For multi-class (mutually exclusive): softmax + categorical cross-entropy. For multi-label (multiple correct): sigmoid + binary cross-entropy per label. Cross-entropy has a nice gradient: p_i - y_i.

statement:
ResNet's residual connections (skip connections) primarily solve which problem in very deep networks?
A) Memory overflow
B) Degradation problem — accuracy saturates and degrades with more layers
C) Slow inference
D) Inability to process images
solution: Without skip connections, adding more layers to a deep network can actually hurt performance (degradation), not just from overfitting but even in training accuracy. Residual connections H(x) = F(x) + x allow the network to learn identity mappings easily (set F(x) = 0) and facilitate gradient flow through the shortcut path, enabling training of networks with 100+ layers.
explanation: The residual formulation makes it easy to learn small refinements rather than complete transformations. ResNet-50 has ~25M parameters and won ImageNet 2015. Modern variants: DenseNet (connects each layer to all subsequent layers), EfficientNet (scales width/depth/resolution together).

statement:
In a Variational Autoencoder (VAE), the ELBO (Evidence Lower BOund) loss consists of:
A) Only reconstruction loss
B) Reconstruction loss + KL divergence between the learned latent distribution and a prior
C) Adversarial loss + reconstruction loss
D) Only KL divergence
solution: VAE loss = Reconstruction loss - KL(q(z|x) || p(z)), where q(z|x) is the encoder's approximate posterior and p(z) is the prior (typically N(0,I)). Reconstruction loss encourages the decoder to reconstruct input well. KL divergence regularizes the latent space to be close to the prior, ensuring smooth interpolation and generation.
explanation: The reparameterization trick z = μ + σ·ε (where ε ~ N(0,I)) makes backpropagation through the sampling step possible. VAEs produce blurry images; GANs produce sharper ones. Diffusion models (DALL-E, Stable Diffusion) have largely superseded both for image generation.

statement:
Why is initializing all neural network weights to zero problematic?
A) It causes exploding gradients
B) All neurons in a layer compute identical gradients, breaking symmetry and preventing learning
C) The network cannot compute a forward pass
D) It leads to very fast but unstable convergence
solution: If all weights are zero, all neurons in a layer produce the same output in the forward pass and receive the same gradient in the backward pass. They remain identical throughout training — a 'symmetry breaking' failure. The network effectively behaves as a single neuron per layer. He/Glorot initialization breaks symmetry with random values.
explanation: He initialization: w ~ N(0, 2/n_in) — designed for ReLU. Glorot/Xavier: w ~ N(0, 2/(n_in+n_out)) — designed for tanh/sigmoid. Proper initialization keeps gradient variance consistent across layers at initialization.

statement:
Compared to full-batch gradient descent, mini-batch stochastic gradient descent (SGD) typically:
A) Always finds better optima
B) Is noisier but can escape local minima and trains faster per epoch
C) Requires more memory
D) Can only be used for classification tasks
solution: Mini-batch SGD uses a random subset (batch) of training data for each update. This introduces noise into gradient estimates, which can actually help escape shallow local minima and saddle points. It also enables GPU parallelism efficiently. Full-batch uses all data — more accurate gradients but very slow for large datasets.
explanation: Typical batch sizes: 32, 64, 128, 256. Larger batches → more accurate gradients, less noisy training, but may generalize worse (sharp minima). Small batches → noisier, better regularization effect, but less GPU efficiency. Learning rate often scales with batch size.

statement:
Word embeddings (like Word2Vec) encode words as dense vectors such that:
A) Each word has a unique one-hot vector
B) Semantically similar words have vectors that are close in the embedding space
C) All words have the same vector magnitude
D) Word vectors are orthogonal to each other
solution: Word2Vec learns embeddings where semantically similar words cluster together. The classic example: vector('King') - vector('Man') + vector('Woman') ≈ vector('Queen'). This arises from training on context: words appearing in similar contexts get similar representations. Dense embeddings (e.g., 300d) are much more efficient than sparse one-hot vectors (vocabulary-size d).
explanation: Word2Vec training: Skip-gram (predict context from word) or CBOW (predict word from context). GloVe uses global co-occurrence statistics. Contextual embeddings (BERT, GPT) produce different vectors for the same word in different contexts — much more powerful.

statement:
A p-value of 0.03 means:
A) There is a 3% probability that the null hypothesis is true
B) There is a 3% probability of observing data at least as extreme as the observed data, assuming the null hypothesis is true
C) The alternative hypothesis is true with 97% probability
D) The effect size is 3% of the population mean
solution: The p-value is the probability of obtaining results at least as extreme as the observed results, given that the null hypothesis is true. P(data | H0). It does NOT measure the probability that H0 is true (that would be P(H0 | data), which requires Bayesian reasoning and a prior). A small p-value means the data is unlikely under H0.
explanation: Common misconceptions about p-values: (1) p-value ≠ P(H0 is true), (2) p < 0.05 doesn't mean the effect is practically significant, (3) non-significant result doesn't prove H0 is true. Effect size (Cohen's d) measures practical significance separately.

statement:
If X ~ N(μ, σ²), approximately what percentage of values fall within one standard deviation of the mean?
A) 50%
B) 68%
C) 95%
D) 99.7%
solution: The empirical rule (68-95-99.7 rule) for the normal distribution: P(μ-σ < X < μ+σ) ≈ 68.3%, P(μ-2σ < X < μ+2σ) ≈ 95.4%, P(μ-3σ < X < μ+3σ) ≈ 99.7%.
explanation: The 68-95-99.7 rule is fundamental for understanding confidence intervals and z-scores. A z-score of ±1.96 captures 95% of the distribution, which is why 95% confidence intervals use z=1.96. Z-score = (x - μ) / σ.

statement:
A disease affects 1% of the population. A test has 99% sensitivity (true positive rate) and 99% specificity (true negative rate). You test positive. What is the probability you actually have the disease?
A) ~99%
B) ~50%
C) ~1%
D) ~33%
solution: Using Bayes' theorem with 10,000 people: 100 have disease, 9900 don't. True positives: 100 × 0.99 = 99. False positives: 9900 × 0.01 = 99. P(disease | positive) = 99 / (99 + 99) = 50%. Even with a 99% accurate test, a rare disease gives 50% PPV because false positives from the large healthy population equal true positives.
explanation: This is the base rate fallacy. PPV = (Sensitivity × Prevalence) / (Sensitivity × Prevalence + (1-Specificity) × (1-Prevalence)). For rare diseases, a positive test is still often a false positive. This is why population screening is complex.

statement:
The Central Limit Theorem states that as sample size n increases, the distribution of the sample mean approaches:
A) The same distribution as the population
B) A normal distribution, regardless of the population distribution
C) A uniform distribution
D) The distribution only if the population is already normal
solution: The CLT states: if X1, X2, ..., Xn are i.i.d. random variables with mean μ and variance σ², then X̄ → N(μ, σ²/n) as n → ∞. This holds regardless of the underlying population distribution (with finite mean and variance). Typically n ≥ 30 is sufficient for good approximation.
explanation: The CLT is why normal distributions appear throughout statistics — many real-world quantities are sums of many small independent effects. It justifies using t-tests and z-tests even for non-normal populations when n is large. Standard error of the mean = σ/√n.

statement:
Pearson correlation coefficient r = 0 indicates:
A) There is definitely no relationship between variables
B) There is no linear relationship, but a non-linear relationship may exist
C) The variables are independent
D) The slope of the regression line is 0
solution: r measures the strength of linear association. r=0 means no linear relationship. However, a perfect non-linear relationship (e.g., Y = X²) can yield r=0 if the data is symmetric around X=0. Independence implies r=0, but r=0 does not imply independence. The classic Anscombe's quartet shows datasets with identical r but very different patterns.
explanation: r ranges from -1 to 1. |r| > 0.7 is often considered strong linear correlation. Spearman's rank correlation is more robust to outliers and captures monotonic (not just linear) relationships. Always visualize data — correlation alone is insufficient.

statement:
A 95% confidence interval for a mean is [42, 58]. What is the correct interpretation?
A) There is a 95% probability that the true population mean is between 42 and 58
B) If we repeated this study many times, 95% of the resulting confidence intervals would contain the true population mean
C) 95% of the data falls between 42 and 58
D) The sample mean has a 95% chance of being between 42 and 58
solution: A confidence interval is a procedure: if we repeat the sampling and interval construction many times, 95% of the intervals produced will contain the true parameter. For any specific interval, the true mean either is or isn't in it — we can't assign probability to a fixed interval containing a fixed (unknown) parameter in the frequentist framework.
explanation: The frequentist vs Bayesian distinction: Bayesian credible intervals (e.g., 'there is 95% probability the parameter is in this interval') directly address what we often want to say, but require prior distributions. Frequentist CIs are about procedure, not probability for a specific interval.

statement:
A researcher sets α = 0.05. They fail to reject the null hypothesis. Later it turns out the null hypothesis was false. What type of error occurred?
A) Type I error (false positive)
B) Type II error (false negative)
C) No error occurred
D) This is a p-hacking error
solution: Type I error (α): reject H0 when H0 is true (false positive). Type II error (β): fail to reject H0 when H0 is false (false negative). Here: H0 was false, but we failed to reject it — that's a Type II error. Power = 1 - β = probability of correctly rejecting a false H0.
explanation: Reducing α (stricter threshold) → fewer Type I errors but more Type II errors. Increasing sample size → reduces Type II errors (increases power) without inflating Type I error rate. Power analysis determines required sample size before collecting data.

statement:
Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) finds model parameters that:
A) Minimize the squared difference between predictions and observations
B) Maximize the probability of observing the given data under the model
C) Maximize the prior probability of the parameters
D) Minimize the number of parameters in the model
solution: MLE maximizes L(θ; X) = P(X | θ) — the likelihood of observing the data X given parameters θ. In practice, we maximize log L (log-likelihood) which is equivalent and numerically stable. For normal distributions, MLE for the mean = sample mean. For logistic regression, MLE leads to cross-entropy loss minimization.
explanation: MAP (Maximum A Posteriori) = MLE + prior = maximizes P(θ|X) ∝ P(X|θ)·P(θ). With a Gaussian prior on weights, MAP is equivalent to L2-regularized MLE. With a Laplace prior, it's equivalent to L1-regularized MLE.

statement:
When comparing multiple models using the same test set repeatedly to select the best one, what problem arises?
A) Underfitting due to limited data
B) The test set effectively becomes a training set, and the selected model is optimistically biased
C) The models become identical over time
D) Computational complexity increases
solution: If you evaluate many models on the same test set and pick the best one, you're implicitly using the test set for selection — overfitting to the test set. The selected model's test performance overestimates true generalization. This is sometimes called 'adaptive data analysis' or 'test set leakage through researcher choices'.
explanation: Best practice: use test set only ONCE at the very end. Use a validation set or cross-validation for model selection. If test set has been used multiple times, consider a fresh holdout set or use statistical corrections (Bonferroni, etc.).

statement:
A fair six-sided die is rolled. What is the expected value of the result?
A) 3
B) 3.5
C) 4
D) 6
solution: E[X] = Σ x·P(X=x) = 1·(1/6) + 2·(1/6) + 3·(1/6) + 4·(1/6) + 5·(1/6) + 6·(1/6) = (1+2+3+4+5+6)/6 = 21/6 = 3.5. Note that 3.5 is not a possible outcome of any single roll — expected value doesn't need to be an achievable outcome.
explanation: Expected value is the long-run average over many trials. E[aX+b] = a·E[X]+b (linearity). For independent variables: E[X+Y] = E[X]+E[Y] (always), E[X·Y] = E[X]·E[Y] (only if independent). Variance: Var(X) = E[X²] - E[X]².

statement:
The bootstrap method estimates the sampling distribution of a statistic by:
A) Assuming the statistic follows a normal distribution
B) Repeatedly resampling with replacement from the observed data and computing the statistic each time
C) Using analytical formulas derived from probability theory
D) Splitting the dataset in half repeatedly
solution: Bootstrap: resample n observations with replacement from the original n observations (creating a 'bootstrap sample') and compute the desired statistic. Repeat B times (e.g., B=1000). The distribution of bootstrap statistics approximates the sampling distribution. Works for any statistic, even those without analytical formulas.
explanation: Bootstrap applications: confidence intervals (percentile method: use 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of bootstrap distribution), standard error estimation, bias estimation. Bootstrap assumes the empirical distribution approximates the true population distribution — works well with n ≥ 30.

statement:
Entropy H(X) = -Σ p(x) log p(x) is maximized when:
A) One outcome has probability 1
B) All outcomes are equally probable
C) The distribution is normal
D) There are only two outcomes
solution: Entropy measures uncertainty/information content. H is maximized by the uniform distribution over n outcomes: H = log(n). If one outcome has probability 1, H = -1·log(1) = 0 (no uncertainty). Uniform distribution over 2 outcomes: H = log(2) = 1 bit. This is why entropy is used as an impurity measure in decision tree splits.
explanation: Shannon entropy (base 2) measures bits of information. KL divergence D(P||Q) = Σ P(x)·log(P(x)/Q(x)) measures distance between distributions (non-symmetric). Cross-entropy H(P,Q) = H(P) + D(P||Q). Minimizing cross-entropy in ML = minimizing KL divergence from model to data distribution.

statement:
ANOVA (Analysis of Variance) is used to test:
A) Whether the variance of a single population equals a specified value
B) Whether the means of three or more groups are significantly different
C) Whether two variables are correlated
D) Whether a distribution is normal
solution: One-way ANOVA tests H0: μ1 = μ2 = ... = μk (all group means are equal) against H1: at least one mean differs. It compares between-group variance to within-group variance via the F-statistic. If groups have similar variance, a large F suggests real differences between group means.
explanation: ANOVA assumptions: independence, normality within groups, homoscedasticity (equal variances — tested with Levene's test). Post-hoc tests (Tukey's HSD, Bonferroni) identify which specific groups differ after a significant ANOVA. Two-way ANOVA tests two factors and their interaction.

statement:
In linear regression, R² = 0.85 means:
A) The model predicts with 85% accuracy
B) 85% of the variance in the target variable is explained by the model
C) The correlation between predictions and actuals is 0.85
D) 85% of predictions are within one standard deviation of the true values
solution: R² = 1 - SS_res/SS_tot, where SS_res = Σ(yi - ŷi)² (residual sum of squares) and SS_tot = Σ(yi - ȳ)² (total sum of squares). R²=0.85 means the model explains 85% of the total variance in y. The remaining 15% is unexplained variance (noise or missing predictors). Note: R² always increases when adding more predictors — adjusted R² penalizes for extra parameters.
explanation: R² is not a percentage accuracy metric. R²=0.85 doesn't mean 85% of predictions are correct. Adjusted R² = 1 - (1-R²)(n-1)/(n-p-1) penalizes model complexity. For non-linear models, R² can be negative (if worse than predicting the mean).

statement:
The Law of Large Numbers states that as sample size increases:
A) The sample variance approaches zero
B) The sample mean converges to the population mean
C) The data becomes normally distributed
D) Individual observations become more predictable
solution: The Law of Large Numbers (LLN): for i.i.d. random variables with finite mean μ, X̄_n → μ as n → ∞ (in probability or almost surely). This is why long-run averages are stable: a fair coin flipped many times approaches 50% heads, though individual flips remain unpredictable.
explanation: Weak LLN: convergence in probability. Strong LLN: almost sure convergence. LLN justifies using sample statistics to estimate population parameters. The Gambler's Fallacy confuses LLN with short-run behavior: past outcomes don't affect future independent trials.

statement:
A function f(x) is convex if:
A) It has exactly one local minimum
B) For any two points x, y: f(λx + (1-λ)y) ≤ λf(x) + (1-λ)f(y) for all λ ∈ [0,1]
C) Its second derivative is always negative
D) It is differentiable everywhere
solution: Convexity: the chord between any two points on the function lies above or on the function (the function curves upward). Geometrically: f lies below the line segment connecting any two points on its graph. For twice-differentiable functions, f is convex iff f''(x) ≥ 0. Convex functions have no local minima that aren't global minima.
explanation: Why convexity matters for ML: convex optimization problems can be solved to global optimality efficiently. Logistic regression, SVMs, Lasso/Ridge are convex. Neural networks are non-convex but empirically still trainable. A function is strictly convex if the inequality is strict (unique global minimum).

statement:
Learning rate warmup in training large neural networks refers to:
A) Decreasing the learning rate at the start of training
B) Starting with a small learning rate and gradually increasing it before decaying
C) Setting a fixed learning rate throughout training
D) Using a larger learning rate for later layers
solution: Warmup: start with small lr (e.g., 0) and linearly increase to target lr over first N steps, then decay (cosine, linear, or step schedule). Early training: model weights are random, gradients are noisy — large lr can destabilize. After warmup, larger lr allows faster progress. Used in BERT, GPT, ViT training.
explanation: Common lr schedules: constant, step decay, cosine annealing, cyclical lr (CLR), 1cycle policy. Cosine annealing: lr = lr_min + (lr_max - lr_min)/2 · (1 + cos(πt/T)). CLR oscillates between lr_min and lr_max, helping escape local minima.

statement:
In constrained optimization, KKT (Karush-Kuhn-Tucker) conditions are necessary conditions for a point to be a local optimum when:
A) The objective function is linear
B) There are equality and/or inequality constraints
C) The problem is unconstrained
D) The Hessian is positive definite
solution: KKT conditions extend Lagrange multiplier conditions to inequality constraints. For minimize f(x) subject to g_i(x) ≤ 0 and h_j(x) = 0, the KKT conditions require: stationarity (∇f + Σλ_i∇g_i + Σμ_j∇h_j = 0), primal feasibility, dual feasibility (λ_i ≥ 0), and complementary slackness (λ_i·g_i(x) = 0). SVMs use KKT conditions in their dual formulation.
explanation: KKT conditions are necessary for any constrained optimum (under constraint qualification assumptions) and sufficient for convex problems. The dual problem of the SVM is derived using KKT conditions and leads to the kernel trick application.

statement:
Random search is often preferred over grid search for hyperparameter optimization because:
A) Random search is always faster in wall-clock time
B) Random search explores more unique values for each hyperparameter when some hyperparameters matter more than others
C) Random search can evaluate more hyperparameter combinations per unit time
D) Grid search cannot handle continuous hyperparameters
solution: In grid search with 5 values per hyperparameter, each hyperparameter only takes 5 distinct values regardless of how many trials. In random search with the same number of trials, each hyperparameter is sampled more broadly. If only 2 of 10 hyperparameters matter, random search explores those 2 more thoroughly. Bergstra & Bengio (2012) showed random search outperforms grid search for this reason.
explanation: Modern approaches: Bayesian optimization (uses surrogate model to select promising regions), Hyperband (successive halving, early stopping of poor configs), ASHA. Libraries: Optuna, Ray Tune, Weights & Biases Sweeps.

statement:
In gradient descent with momentum, the velocity term:
A) Speeds up learning in all directions equally
B) Accumulates gradients over time, accelerating in consistent directions and dampening oscillations
C) Adapts the learning rate per parameter
D) Clips gradients to prevent explosion
solution: Momentum: v_t = β·v_{t-1} + ∇L, w = w - α·v_t. The velocity v accumulates past gradients with decay factor β (typically 0.9). In directions where gradients consistently point the same way, velocity builds up (faster progress). In oscillating directions, gradients cancel out (dampening). Analogy: a ball rolling downhill gains momentum.
explanation: Nesterov momentum: compute gradient at 'lookahead' position w - α·β·v rather than current position — more accurate update. Both reduce oscillations in steep ravines (common in ML loss landscapes). SGD + momentum + weight decay is still competitive with Adam for image classification.

statement:
In neural network optimization, saddle points are:
A) Local minima that are not global minima
B) Points where the gradient is zero but the point is a minimum in some directions and a maximum in others
C) Points where the Hessian has all positive eigenvalues
D) Flat regions with zero gradient throughout
solution: A saddle point has zero gradient (critical point) but is neither a local min nor max — the Hessian has both positive and negative eigenvalues. In high-dimensional neural networks, saddle points are far more common than local minima. SGD noise and momentum help escape saddle points. True local minima (all Hessian eigenvalues positive) are relatively rare in deep networks.
explanation: Loss landscape research (Goodfellow et al., Li et al.) shows: (1) most critical points in deep networks are saddle points, (2) local minima tend to have similar loss values to the global minimum, (3) the loss landscape has many 'flat' regions. This partly explains why neural networks are trainable despite non-convexity.

statement:
Gradient clipping is used in training RNNs primarily to address:
A) Vanishing gradients
B) Exploding gradients
C) Slow convergence
D) Overfitting
solution: Gradient clipping rescales gradients when their norm exceeds a threshold: if ||g|| > threshold, g = g × threshold/||g||. This prevents exploding gradients (gradient norms growing exponentially in deep/recurrent networks) from causing catastrophically large weight updates. It doesn't address vanishing gradients — that requires architectural solutions like LSTM or skip connections.
explanation: Norm clipping (clip the entire gradient vector) is preferred over value clipping (clip each component independently) as it preserves gradient direction. Typical threshold: 1.0 to 5.0. In practice: monitor gradient norms during training; sudden spikes indicate exploding gradients.

statement:
Newton's method for optimization converges faster than gradient descent because it:
A) Uses a larger learning rate
B) Uses second-order (curvature) information to scale the gradient step appropriately for each direction
C) Is less sensitive to the choice of learning rate
D) Avoids local minima by jumping over them
solution: Newton's method: w = w - H^(-1)·g, where H is the Hessian (matrix of second derivatives) and g is the gradient. The inverse Hessian scales the gradient: in flat directions (small curvature), take larger steps; in steep directions (large curvature), take smaller steps. This achieves quadratic convergence near the optimum vs linear convergence for gradient descent.
explanation: Newton's method drawbacks: computing and inverting H is O(n³) for n parameters — infeasible for large networks. Quasi-Newton methods (L-BFGS) approximate H^(-1) using gradient history. Natural gradient methods use the Fisher information matrix instead of Hessian.

statement:
Cosine annealing learning rate schedule is characterized by:
A) Constant learning rate throughout training
B) Monotonically decreasing learning rate
C) Smooth oscillation between maximum and minimum learning rates following a cosine curve
D) Randomly chosen learning rates at each step
solution: Cosine annealing: lr(t) = lr_min + (lr_max - lr_min)/2 · (1 + cos(πt/T_max)), where t is current step and T_max is the period. lr decreases smoothly from lr_max to lr_min then restarts. With warm restarts (SGDR), periodic restarts help explore different loss basins and can improve final performance via 'snapshot ensembling'.
explanation: Cyclical learning rate schedules (Smith, 2017) and cosine annealing with warm restarts (SGDR, Loshchilov & Hutter, 2017) are widely used. The 1cycle policy (fast.ai) uses one cycle of warmup + cosine decay and achieves strong results with fewer epochs.

statement:
Early stopping in neural network training:
A) Stops training when training loss reaches zero
B) Stops training when validation loss stops improving, preventing overfitting
C) Reduces the learning rate when training stalls
D) Removes neurons that haven't learned useful features
solution: Early stopping monitors validation loss during training. When validation loss stops decreasing (or starts increasing) for a specified number of epochs (patience), training stops and the model from the best validation epoch is restored. This is a simple but effective regularization technique — it implicitly limits model complexity.
explanation: Early stopping is equivalent to L2 regularization under certain conditions. Patience: how many epochs to wait after validation loss stops improving. Too small patience → stops too early; too large → trains longer, wasting time but not necessarily hurting performance. Model checkpoint: save weights when validation loss improves.

statement:
Weight decay (L2 regularization in the optimizer) is equivalent to:
A) Reducing the learning rate
B) Adding a penalty λ||w||² to the loss function, penalizing large weights
C) Zeroing out small weights
D) Clipping weight values
solution: Weight decay adds λ||w||² to the loss: L_total = L_task + λ·Σwi². The gradient becomes ∂L/∂wi = ∂L_task/∂wi + 2λwi. The weight update: wi = wi - α·(gradient + 2λwi) = (1 - 2αλ)wi - α·gradient. The factor (1 - 2αλ) < 1 decays weights toward zero at each step. λ controls regularization strength.
explanation: Note: in adaptive optimizers (Adam), weight decay ≠ L2 regularization due to the adaptive scaling. AdamW (Loshchilov & Hutter, 2019) decouples weight decay from the gradient update, applying it directly to weights — empirically superior for Transformers.

statement:
Coordinate descent optimization iteratively minimizes the objective by:
A) Computing the full gradient and updating all parameters simultaneously
B) Updating one parameter (or group) at a time while holding others fixed
C) Randomly selecting a learning rate at each step
D) Using the second derivative to determine step size
solution: Coordinate descent: at each iteration, select one coordinate (parameter) and minimize the objective along that dimension while keeping all other parameters fixed. Repeat for all coordinates cyclically or randomly. This is the basis of the Lasso solution algorithm (LARS) and SVM training (SMO algorithm). Each sub-problem may have a closed-form solution.
explanation: Block coordinate descent updates groups of parameters. Stochastic coordinate descent updates randomly selected coordinates. The SMO (Sequential Minimal Optimization) algorithm for SVMs solves the smallest possible QP problem (2 variables) at each step, making SVM training tractable.

statement:
He initialization sets initial weights to be drawn from N(0, 2/n_in) rather than N(0, 1/n_in) because:
A) It produces larger initial outputs for better gradient flow
B) It accounts for the variance reduction caused by ReLU zeroing out half the neurons
C) It is computationally more efficient
D) It ensures weights sum to zero
solution: For a ReLU network, approximately half the pre-activation values are negative and set to zero by ReLU, roughly halving the variance. To maintain consistent gradient variance across layers, the weight variance needs to be doubled compared to linear activation: Var(w) = 2/n_in. Glorot/Xavier uses 2/(n_in+n_out) for tanh/sigmoid where no similar zeroing occurs.
explanation: He initialization: for ReLU networks. Glorot/Xavier: for tanh, sigmoid networks. LeCun: for SELU (self-normalizing networks). Orthogonal initialization: useful for RNNs. Proper initialization prevents activation values from exponentially growing or shrinking with depth.

statement:
Bayesian optimization for hyperparameter search uses a surrogate model (e.g., Gaussian Process) to:
A) Directly compute the gradient of the validation loss with respect to hyperparameters
B) Model the objective function and use an acquisition function to select the next hyperparameter configuration to evaluate
C) Train multiple models in parallel on different data subsets
D) Automatically determine the optimal number of training epochs
solution: Bayesian optimization: maintains a surrogate model (typically Gaussian Process) that estimates the objective function mean and uncertainty. An acquisition function (EI, UCB, Thompson sampling) balances exploitation (high predicted performance) and exploration (high uncertainty). The next configuration to evaluate is chosen by maximizing the acquisition function — much more sample-efficient than random or grid search.
explanation: Acquisition functions: Expected Improvement (EI) = E[max(f(x) - f_best, 0)], Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) = μ(x) + κσ(x). Bayesian opt works well for expensive evaluations (few hundred) but poorly for very high-dimensional spaces (>20 dims). Tree-structured Parzen Estimator (TPE, used in Hyperopt/Optuna) is a scalable alternative.

statement:
Adagrad adapts the learning rate per parameter by dividing by the square root of the sum of squared past gradients. This causes:
A) Parameters with large gradients to receive larger updates
B) Parameters with large gradients to receive smaller updates (and vice versa)
C) All parameters to eventually have the same effective learning rate
D) The learning rate to increase monotonically over time
solution: Adagrad: w_i = w_i - α / (√G_i + ε) · g_i, where G_i = Σ_{t} g_{i,t}². Parameters with large historical gradients (frequent features) get small effective lr; parameters with small gradients get large effective lr. Good for sparse features (NLP). Problem: G accumulates indefinitely, causing lr to shrink to near-zero — training can stop prematurely. RMSProp fixes this with exponential decay.
explanation: Adagrad → RMSProp (exponential decay of G) → Adam (adds momentum). Adagrad works well for NLP tasks with sparse gradients but poorly for dense deep learning. The learning rate shrinks monotonically which is a fundamental limitation.

statement:
You have a dataset where 30% of values in a feature are missing. Which imputation strategy is most likely to introduce bias?
A) Multiple imputation
B) Replacing missing values with the mean
C) Using a model to predict missing values
D) Removing rows with missing values when missingness is completely at random (MCAR)
solution: Mean imputation replaces missing values with the feature mean. This artificially reduces the variance of the feature, distorts correlations with other features, and biases estimates if data is not MCAR (Missing Completely at Random). Multiple imputation creates multiple complete datasets with different imputed values, preserving uncertainty. Model-based imputation uses feature correlations but can overfit.
explanation: Missing data mechanisms: MCAR (missingness unrelated to data), MAR (missingness depends on observed data), MNAR (missingness depends on unobserved data). MNAR is the most problematic. Multiple imputation (MICE) is the gold standard for MAR data.

statement:
For a categorical feature 'Color' with values {Red, Green, Blue}, one-hot encoding creates:
A) One column with values 1, 2, 3
B) Three binary columns: is_Red, is_Green, is_Blue
C) One column with values 0, 0.5, 1
D) Log-transformed counts of each category
solution: One-hot encoding creates a binary column for each category value. [Red, Green, Blue, Red] becomes [[1,0,0], [0,1,0], [0,0,1], [1,0,0]]. This avoids implying ordinal relationships (1 < 2 < 3 is false for colors). For high-cardinality features, one-hot creates very sparse, wide matrices — consider target encoding or embeddings instead.
explanation: Encoding options: ordinal (for ordered categories), one-hot (nominal low-cardinality), target/mean encoding (replace with mean target value — risk of overfitting), frequency encoding, binary encoding, embeddings (for high cardinality in neural networks). Drop one column to avoid perfect multicollinearity (dummy variable trap).

statement:
Min-max normalization scales features to [0, 1] using x' = (x - min) / (max - min). What is a key disadvantage compared to standardization (z-score)?
A) Min-max is slower to compute
B) Min-max is highly sensitive to outliers that affect the min and max values
C) Min-max cannot handle negative values
D) Min-max requires the data to be normally distributed
solution: Min-max uses the minimum and maximum values, which are the most extreme points — extremely sensitive to outliers. A single outlier can compress all other values into a tiny range. Z-score standardization uses mean and standard deviation, which are more robust (though still affected by outliers). For robust scaling, use median and IQR (RobustScaler in scikit-learn).
explanation: Min-max: use when algorithm requires bounded inputs (neural networks with sigmoid output, image pixel values 0-255 → 0-1). Z-score: use for most ML algorithms, especially when distribution is approximately normal. RobustScaler: use when outliers are present.

statement:
Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE) selects features by:
A) Selecting features with correlation above a threshold
B) Iteratively training a model, removing the least important feature, and repeating until the desired number of features remains
C) Using mutual information between features and target
D) Principal component analysis to identify important directions
solution: RFE: (1) Train model on all features, (2) rank features by importance, (3) remove the least important feature, (4) repeat until desired number of features. The model defines 'importance' (weights for linear models, feature importance for trees). This accounts for feature interactions since remaining features may compensate for removed ones.
explanation: Feature selection methods: filter (statistical test, correlation — fast, ignores model), wrapper (RFE, forward/backward selection — uses model performance, expensive), embedded (Lasso, tree importance — model learns which features to use). More features isn't always better: curse of dimensionality, computational cost, overfitting risk.

statement:
Data leakage occurs when information from the test set (or future data) is inadvertently used during training. Which of the following is a subtle example of data leakage?
A) Using test data for final evaluation
B) Fitting a StandardScaler on the entire dataset before splitting into train/test
C) Using stratified sampling for train/test split
D) Computing training accuracy
solution: Fitting the scaler on the entire dataset means the test set's mean and variance influence the scaling applied to the training data — information about test points has 'leaked' into training. Correct approach: fit scaler only on training data, apply (transform) to both train and test. Same applies to imputers, encoders, PCA, and any preprocessing step.
explanation: Common leakage sources: preprocessing on full dataset, using future information as features (time series), features computed from target, copies of target in features. Leakage causes overly optimistic evaluation and poor production performance. Always use pipelines (sklearn Pipeline) to prevent leakage.

statement:
The IQR (Interquartile Range) method identifies outliers as values:
A) More than 2 standard deviations from the mean
B) Below Q1 - 1.5×IQR or above Q3 + 1.5×IQR
C) In the bottom or top 5% of the distribution
D) Outside the range [μ-3σ, μ+3σ]
solution: IQR = Q3 - Q1 (middle 50% of data). Outlier boundaries: lower = Q1 - 1.5×IQR, upper = Q3 + 1.5×IQR. This is the basis of the box plot whiskers. The factor 1.5 was chosen by Tukey to capture about 99.3% of data from a normal distribution (similar to ±2.7σ). The IQR method is more robust than z-score since it doesn't use mean/std (which are themselves sensitive to outliers).
explanation: Outlier treatment options: remove (if genuine errors), cap/winsorize (replace with boundary value), transform (log transform reduces right-skew), use robust algorithms (tree-based methods, MAE loss). Never remove outliers blindly — they may be the most important observations.

statement:
SMOTE (Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique) handles class imbalance by:
A) Duplicating minority class samples exactly
B) Creating synthetic minority samples by interpolating between existing minority samples and their k-nearest neighbors
C) Removing majority class samples randomly
D) Assigning higher weights to minority class during training
solution: SMOTE selects a minority sample, finds its k-nearest minority neighbors, and creates synthetic samples along the line segments connecting them: x_new = x_i + λ·(x_nn - x_i) where λ ~ Uniform(0,1). This creates new, varied minority samples rather than exact duplicates (which would cause overfitting). Should only be applied to training data, never test data.
explanation: Class imbalance techniques: oversampling (SMOTE, ADASYN), undersampling (random, Tomek links), class weights (cost-sensitive learning), threshold adjustment, ensemble methods (BalancedRandomForest, EasyEnsemble). Each has tradeoffs. No single method is universally best.

statement:
Feature crossing (interaction features) involves:
A) Normalizing two features to have the same scale
B) Creating a new feature as the product or combination of two existing features to capture non-linear relationships
C) Removing one of two highly correlated features
D) Averaging two features into one
solution: Feature crossing creates new features encoding interactions: x1×x2, x1/x2, or categorical combinations. Example: 'income' × 'age' captures that the effect of income on spending may differ by age group. Linear models cannot capture such interactions without explicit feature crossing. Polynomial features are systematic feature crossing up to degree d.
explanation: Feature crossing is important for linear models (logistic regression, linear SVM) that can't learn interactions natively. Tree-based models learn interactions automatically. Neural networks with enough capacity also learn interactions. Deep & Cross Networks explicitly learn feature crosses up to high order.

statement:
When building features from a timestamp for a machine learning model, which set of features is most appropriate?
A) The raw timestamp as a single integer
B) Hour of day, day of week, month, is_weekend, is_holiday — cyclical/categorical time components
C) Time since epoch in milliseconds
D) A random hash of the timestamp
solution: Raw timestamps as integers encode linear time but not cyclical patterns: hour 23 and hour 0 are adjacent but far apart as integers. Extracting cyclical features (with sin/cos encoding for cyclical ones) captures time patterns: seasonality, weekly cycles, business hours. is_weekend and is_holiday capture calendar events. For cyclical features: encode_hour = (sin(2π·hour/24), cos(2π·hour/24)).
explanation: Time series feature engineering: lag features (past values at t-1, t-7, t-30), rolling statistics (mean, std, min, max over window), time since event, Fourier features for seasonality. Proper handling of temporal structure requires time-based train/test splits, not random splits.

statement:
The 'curse of dimensionality' refers to:
A) The computational cost of storing high-dimensional data
B) As dimensions increase, data becomes increasingly sparse and distances lose meaning, requiring exponentially more data for reliable estimates
C) The inability of neural networks to process high-dimensional inputs
D) The overfitting that occurs with many features in any model
solution: In d dimensions, the volume of space grows as r^d. To maintain the same sample density, data requirements grow exponentially with d. Additionally, in high dimensions all points are approximately equidistant — nearest neighbor methods break down. A unit hypercube in d=100 dimensions has most of its 'volume' in the corners. Sparsity and distance concentration make many ML algorithms less effective.
explanation: Mitigation: dimensionality reduction (PCA, t-SNE, autoencoders), feature selection, regularization, domain knowledge. The 'blessing of dimensionality' is that high-dimensional data often lies on low-dimensional manifolds — deep learning exploits this. Practical rule: need at least 5-10 samples per feature for linear models.

statement:
In a CNN for image classification, what does a convolutional layer's filter (kernel) learn to detect?
A) Global statistics of the entire image
B) Local spatial patterns such as edges, textures, and shapes
C) Pixel intensity histograms
D) Color distribution across the image
solution: Convolutional filters are small matrices that slide over the input image computing dot products. Early layer filters learn low-level features (edges, corners, colors). Middle layers combine these into textures and parts. Deep layers detect high-level features (faces, objects). The key property is weight sharing: the same filter is applied everywhere, making CNNs translationally equivariant and parameter-efficient.
explanation: A 3×3 filter has 9 weights (plus bias) — compared to a fully-connected layer with width×height weights per neuron. A 224×224 image with 64 filters per layer: Conv layer has 64×(3×3×3) = 1,728 parameters; equivalent FC would have 224×224×3 = 150,528 weights per neuron.

statement:
Data augmentation in image tasks creates additional training samples by:
A) Downloading more images from the internet
B) Applying label-preserving transformations such as rotations, flips, crops, and color jitter
C) Removing low-quality images from the dataset
D) Reducing image resolution to speed up training
solution: Data augmentation applies random transformations that change the image but not its label: horizontal flip, rotation (±15°), random crop, brightness/contrast change, Gaussian noise, etc. This artificially expands the dataset and improves generalization. It acts as a regularizer by preventing the model from memorizing specific pixel patterns.
explanation: Advanced augmentation: Mixup (blend two images and labels), CutMix (paste crop from one image into another), AutoAugment (learned augmentation policies), RandAugment (simplified random augmentation). Test-time augmentation (TTA): apply augmentation at inference and average predictions.

statement:
In object detection, Intersection over Union (IoU) measures:
A) The probability that an object is present in an image
B) The overlap between predicted and ground-truth bounding boxes as area(intersection)/area(union)
C) The number of objects detected per image
D) The confidence score of the detection model
solution: IoU = area(predicted ∩ ground_truth) / area(predicted ∪ ground_truth). IoU ∈ [0, 1]. IoU = 1 means perfect overlap. IoU = 0 means no overlap. Typically IoU ≥ 0.5 is considered a correct detection. Mean Average Precision (mAP) at various IoU thresholds (e.g., COCO uses mAP@[0.5:0.05:0.95]) is the standard object detection metric.
explanation: Non-Maximum Suppression (NMS) uses IoU: when multiple boxes predict the same object, keep the highest-confidence box and suppress overlapping boxes (IoU > threshold). Anchor-based detection (YOLO, SSD, Faster RCNN) predicts offsets from anchor boxes. Anchor-free detection (FCOS, CenterNet) predicts object centers directly.

statement:
The difference between semantic segmentation and instance segmentation is:
A) Semantic segmentation is faster; instance segmentation is more accurate
B) Semantic segmentation labels each pixel with a class; instance segmentation also distinguishes between different instances of the same class
C) Semantic segmentation works on videos; instance segmentation works on images
D) Instance segmentation uses bounding boxes; semantic segmentation uses pixel masks
solution: Semantic segmentation: every pixel gets a class label (car, road, person) but doesn't distinguish car1 from car2. Instance segmentation: every pixel gets a class AND an instance ID — car1 and car2 are separately identified. Panoptic segmentation combines both: semantic for 'stuff' (sky, road) and instance for 'things' (car, person).
explanation: Key models: Semantic: FCN, DeepLab, SegNet. Instance: Mask R-CNN (extends Faster R-CNN with mask branch), YOLACT. Panoptic: Panoptic FPN, Mask2Former. Applications: autonomous driving (pixel-level scene understanding), medical imaging (organ/tumor segmentation).

statement:
A ResNet-50 model pre-trained on ImageNet (1000 classes) needs to be adapted for a binary medical image classification task (normal vs. abnormal). The most common fine-tuning approach is to:
A) Train the entire ResNet-50 from random initialization on medical images
B) Replace the final classification layer with a new binary output layer and fine-tune the network
C) Use ResNet-50's embeddings directly without any training on medical data
D) Remove all convolutional layers and only fine-tune the batch normalization parameters
solution: Standard approach: remove the final 1000-class FC layer, add a new 2-class (or 1-class with sigmoid) output layer initialized randomly. Fine-tune: (1) first train only the new head with other layers frozen, then (2) unfreeze some/all layers and fine-tune with a small learning rate. This preserves learned feature representations while adapting to the new task.
explanation: Domain similarity matters: ImageNet → natural images transfer well. ImageNet → medical images: early layers still useful (edge detection), later layers may need more fine-tuning. With very little data (<100 images): freeze all convolutional layers, train only head. With more data: progressive unfreezing from top layers down.

statement:
Vision Transformers (ViT) process images by:
A) Using convolutional layers followed by a transformer encoder
B) Splitting the image into fixed-size patches, treating each patch as a token, and applying standard transformer self-attention
C) Applying self-attention pixel by pixel
D) Using a recurrent network to process image rows sequentially
solution: ViT divides an image into N patches (e.g., 16×16 pixels each), linearly embeds each patch into a token, adds position embeddings, and processes the sequence with a standard Transformer encoder. A [CLS] token is prepended and its output representation is used for classification. For 224×224 images with 16×16 patches: N = (224/16)² = 196 patches.
explanation: ViT requires large datasets to outperform CNNs (CNNs have built-in translation invariance as an inductive bias; ViT must learn this from data). DeiT uses knowledge distillation to train ViT with less data. Hybrid models combine CNN feature extractor with Transformer. Swin Transformer uses hierarchical windows for efficiency.

statement:
In a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN), what is the role of the discriminator?
A) Generate realistic images from random noise
B) Distinguish between real images from the dataset and fake images from the generator
C) Encode images into a latent representation
D) Classify generated images into categories
solution: GAN minimax game: Generator G tries to fool discriminator D by generating realistic images. Discriminator D tries to correctly classify real vs. fake. Objective: min_G max_D E[log D(x)] + E[log(1-D(G(z)))]. At equilibrium, G generates the data distribution and D outputs 0.5 for all inputs. Training is adversarial and notoriously unstable.
explanation: GAN problems: mode collapse (generates only a few types), training instability. Solutions: Wasserstein GAN (WGAN) uses Earth Mover's distance for more stable training; spectral normalization, progressive growing (ProGAN), StyleGAN (style-based generator). Modern image synthesis uses diffusion models which have surpassed GANs in quality.

statement:
Why are image pixels typically normalized (divided by 255 or using mean/std subtraction) before feeding to a neural network?
A) To reduce image file size
B) To ensure consistent scale that helps gradient-based optimization converge faster and more stably
C) To remove color information from the image
D) To make the network architecture simpler
solution: Raw pixel values are integers in [0, 255]. Large input values can cause large activations in the first layer, requiring very small weights to compensate — this can cause slow convergence or numerical instability. Normalizing to [0,1] or standardizing with ImageNet mean/std keeps activations in a well-conditioned range for gradient-based optimization.
explanation: ImageNet mean: [0.485, 0.456, 0.406] (RGB), std: [0.229, 0.224, 0.225]. When using pre-trained models, use the same normalization as used in pre-training. For training from scratch, use dataset-specific statistics. Normalization is part of the data preprocessing pipeline, not learnable.

statement:
The receptive field of a neuron in a CNN refers to:
A) The set of filters applied to the neuron's input
B) The region of the original input image that influences the neuron's output
C) The number of channels in the feature map
D) The spatial resolution of the neuron's feature map
solution: The receptive field is the input region a neuron 'sees'. With 3×3 convolutions: layer 1 neurons see 3×3 input. Layer 2 neurons see 5×5 input. Layer k sees (2k+1)×(2k+1). Deep networks with many small filters achieve large receptive fields while maintaining computational efficiency. Dilated/atrous convolutions expand receptive fields without adding parameters.
explanation: Effective receptive field: not all input pixels in the theoretical RF contribute equally — central pixels dominate. For tasks needing global context (image captioning), attention mechanisms or global average pooling are more effective. Stride > 1 and pooling also increase the receptive field per layer.

statement:
For image classification, top-5 accuracy means:
A) Accuracy on the top 5% hardest examples
B) The correct label is within the model's 5 highest-probability predictions
C) Accuracy measured on 5 different test sets
D) Average accuracy across 5 cross-validation folds
solution: Top-5 accuracy: a prediction is correct if the ground-truth label appears in the top 5 predicted classes (by probability). This was the standard metric for ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge (ILSVRC). Human-level top-5 error is ~5.1%. AlexNet (2012) achieved 15.3%, ResNet (2015) achieved 3.57% — surpassing human performance.
explanation: Top-5 accuracy is forgiving for tasks where multiple labels could be valid (e.g., Labrador and dog breeds). Top-1 accuracy measures if the single highest-probability prediction is correct. For production systems, latency (inference time), model size, and robustness to distribution shift are also critical metrics.

statement:
Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) tokenization works by:
A) Splitting text on whitespace and punctuation
B) Iteratively merging the most frequent pair of tokens until reaching a target vocabulary size
C) Mapping each word to a unique integer
D) Splitting words into individual characters
solution: BPE starts with character-level vocabulary and iteratively merges the most frequent adjacent token pair. After many merges, common words become single tokens; rare words are split into subword units. This handles out-of-vocabulary words gracefully — any word can be decomposed into known subword pieces. Used in GPT-2, GPT-3, RoBERTa.
explanation: Comparison: word-level (large vocab, OOV problem), character-level (small vocab, long sequences), subword (balance). SentencePiece (used in BERT multilingual, T5) is language-agnostic. WordPiece (BERT) is similar to BPE but uses likelihood instead of frequency for merges.

statement:
Perplexity is a standard metric for language model evaluation. Lower perplexity indicates:
A) The model is slower at generating text
B) The model assigns higher probability to the test text — better predictions
C) The vocabulary size is smaller
D) The model has fewer parameters
solution: Perplexity = 2^(-1/N · Σ log2 P(wi|w1,...,wi-1)) = exp(cross-entropy). It measures how 'surprised' the model is by the test text — lower is better. A perplexity of 1 means perfect prediction. A perplexity of V (vocabulary size) means the model is no better than uniform distribution. Modern LLMs achieve perplexity < 10 on standard benchmarks.
explanation: Perplexity is dataset-dependent — can't compare across different tokenizations or test sets. It measures calibration of probability estimates. For GPT-style models, perplexity is directly related to training loss (cross-entropy). Limitations: doesn't directly measure output quality or factual accuracy.

statement:
BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers) is pre-trained using which objectives?
A) Next-token prediction and sentence ordering
B) Masked Language Modeling (MLM) and Next Sentence Prediction (NSP)
C) Text classification and named entity recognition
D) Machine translation and summarization
solution: MLM: 15% of tokens are randomly masked; BERT predicts the original masked tokens using context from both directions (bidirectional). This allows BERT to learn deep bidirectional representations, unlike GPT which is unidirectional. NSP: BERT predicts whether sentence B naturally follows sentence A (50% real pairs, 50% random). NSP was later found less critical (RoBERTa removed it).
explanation: BERT architecture: Transformer encoder (bidirectional). GPT: Transformer decoder (unidirectional, autoregressive). T5: encoder-decoder, frames all tasks as text-to-text. BERT is better for understanding tasks (classification, QA, NER). GPT is better for generation tasks (text completion, summarization).

statement:
In sequence-to-sequence models with attention, what problem does attention solve that vanilla encoder-decoder models have?
A) Attention reduces the number of parameters in the model
B) Vanilla encoder-decoder compresses all source information into a fixed-size vector; attention allows the decoder to access all encoder hidden states directly
C) Attention enables processing of longer vocabularies
D) Attention speeds up training by reducing gradient computation
