solution: In vanilla encoder-decoder, all source information is compressed into a single fixed-size context vector — information bottleneck for long sequences. The decoder can only access this one summary. With attention (Bahdanau, 2015), the decoder can attend to all encoder hidden states at each step, computing a context vector as a weighted sum — different positions get different attention weights based on relevance.
explanation: Attention weight for position i: α_i = softmax(score(decoder_state, encoder_hidden_i)). Common score functions: dot product, bilinear, additive (Bahdanau). Self-attention in Transformers allows each token to attend to all other tokens. Multi-head attention learns multiple attention patterns simultaneously.

statement:
TF-IDF (Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency) gives low weight to words that:
A) Appear rarely in a document
B) Appear in many documents across the corpus (common words)
C) Are long or contain special characters
D) Appear at the beginning of documents
solution: TF-IDF = TF × IDF. TF = count of word in document / total words in document (how important word is to this document). IDF = log(N / df) where N = total documents, df = documents containing the word (penalizes words appearing in many documents). Words like 'the', 'a', 'is' appear in nearly all documents → very low IDF → low TF-IDF weight.
explanation: TF-IDF is the classic text feature representation before deep learning. It creates sparse, high-dimensional vectors (one dimension per vocabulary word). Better than raw word counts — removes stop word bias. Limitations: ignores word order, no semantic understanding. Word embeddings and contextual representations (BERT) are more powerful but require more data.

statement:
In BIO tagging for Named Entity Recognition, the tag 'B-PER' means:
A) The token is at the Bottom of a PERSON entity
B) The token is at the Beginning of a PERSON entity span
C) The token Belongs to any named entity
D) The token is a Boundary between two entities
solution: BIO tagging: B (Beginning) = first token of an entity, I (Inside) = subsequent tokens of the same entity, O (Outside) = not an entity. Example: 'Barack Obama visited Paris' → B-PER, I-PER, O, B-LOC. BIOES extends this: B, I, O, E (End), S (Single token entity). Sequence labeling models predict one tag per token.
explanation: NER approaches: rule-based, CRF (Conditional Random Field — classic ML), BiLSTM-CRF (deep learning), fine-tuned BERT (state-of-the-art). BIO ensures valid entity spans: an I tag can only follow B or I of the same entity type. Applications: information extraction, knowledge graph construction, document processing.

statement:
Aspect-based sentiment analysis differs from standard sentiment analysis by:
A) Being faster and requiring less data
B) Identifying sentiment toward specific aspects or attributes of an entity, not just overall sentiment
C) Only working on social media text
D) Using unsupervised rather than supervised learning
solution: Standard sentiment: 'The camera is excellent but battery life is terrible' → mixed/neutral. Aspect-based: camera aspect → positive, battery_life aspect → negative. This provides more granular information. Tasks: aspect detection (what aspects are mentioned), aspect sentiment classification (what sentiment toward each aspect).
explanation: Applications: product review analysis (which features customers like/dislike), survey analysis, competitive intelligence. Challenge: implicit aspects ('The phone died after 2 hours' → negative battery sentiment without mentioning battery). SemEval has organized multiple ABSA shared tasks.

statement:
BLEU score for machine translation evaluation measures:
A) Semantic similarity between translation and reference using embeddings
B) N-gram precision between the generated translation and reference translations, with a brevity penalty
C) Human-rated fluency and adequacy on a 1-5 scale
D) Word error rate between generated and reference translations
solution: BLEU (Bilingual Evaluation Understudy): computes precision of 1-grams, 2-grams, 3-grams, 4-grams between hypothesis and one or more references, then takes geometric mean and applies brevity penalty (penalizes short translations). BLEU ∈ [0,1]. 0 = no n-gram overlap, 1 = perfect match. Commercial systems score ~40-50 BLEU.
explanation: BLEU limitations: doesn't measure recall (important for coverage), insensitive to meaning (synonym can't substitute), sentence-level correlation with humans is weak. Alternatives: ROUGE (recall-oriented, used for summarization), METEOR (considers synonyms, stemming), BERTScore (semantic similarity via BERT embeddings), human evaluation is gold standard.

statement:
Positional encodings in the original Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017) use sine and cosine functions of different frequencies. Why are positional encodings necessary?
A) To reduce computational complexity of attention
B) Transformers process all tokens in parallel and self-attention is permutation-invariant — without positional encodings the model cannot determine token order
C) To enable the model to handle sequences longer than training data
D) To prevent vanishing gradients during backpropagation
solution: Self-attention computes the same output regardless of token order (permutation-invariant). 'The cat sat' and 'sat The cat' would produce identical attention weights without position information. Positional encodings add position-dependent signals to token embeddings: PE(pos, 2i) = sin(pos/10000^(2i/d)), PE(pos, 2i+1) = cos(pos/10000^(2i/d)). Each position gets a unique encoding.
explanation: Sine/cosine choice: deterministic (no training needed), allows model to generalize to unseen positions, relative positions can be recovered (PE(pos+k) is a linear function of PE(pos)). Learned positional embeddings (BERT) are also common. RoPE (Rotary Position Embedding, LLaMA) and ALiBi encode relative positions more directly.

statement:
Hallucination in large language models refers to:
A) Models generating text in languages not seen during training
B) Models generating fluent, confident text that is factually incorrect or fabricated
C) Models refusing to answer certain questions
D) Models copying training data verbatim
solution: LLMs are trained to generate plausible next tokens, not to be factually correct. They can generate confident, grammatically correct text with fabricated facts, fake citations, non-existent people, or incorrect numerical claims. This happens because the model has learned surface patterns of fluent text rather than grounded factual knowledge.
explanation: Mitigation approaches: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG — ground answers in retrieved documents), fine-tuning on curated factual data, RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback — penalize hallucination), chain-of-thought prompting, uncertainty quantification. Hallucination is an active research area with no complete solution.

statement:
In reinforcement learning, the agent learns by:
A) Being given correct answers for every action
B) Receiving reward signals from the environment and updating a policy to maximize cumulative reward
C) Copying the behavior of expert demonstrations
D) Minimizing a fixed loss function like supervised learning
solution: RL framework: agent in state s takes action a (from policy π), transitions to state s' and receives reward r from environment. Goal: find policy π* that maximizes expected cumulative (discounted) reward: E[Σγ^t · r_t]. Unlike supervised learning, there's no direct supervision — only reward signals that may be sparse, delayed, or noisy.
explanation: Key components: state space S, action space A, reward function R, transition dynamics P(s'|s,a), discount factor γ ∈ [0,1]. RL has explored applications including: game playing (AlphaGo, Atari), robotics, dialog systems, RLHF for LLMs, recommendation systems.

statement:
In Q-learning, Q(s, a) represents:
A) The probability of taking action a in state s
B) The expected cumulative discounted reward of taking action a in state s and then following the optimal policy
C) The immediate reward of taking action a in state s
D) The transition probability to the next state
solution: Q(s,a) = E[r_t + γ·r_{t+1} + γ²·r_{t+2} + ... | s_t=s, a_t=a, following π* thereafter]. The Bellman equation: Q*(s,a) = E[r + γ · max_{a'} Q*(s',a')]. Q-learning update: Q(s,a) ← Q(s,a) + α[r + γ·max_{a'} Q(s',a') - Q(s,a)]. Optimal policy: π*(s) = argmax_a Q*(s,a).
explanation: Q-learning is off-policy (can learn from any experience). Deep Q-Network (DQN, DeepMind 2013): uses neural network to approximate Q(s,a). Key innovations: experience replay (breaks temporal correlations), target network (stable training targets). Achieved human-level performance on 49 Atari games.

statement:
The exploration-exploitation trade-off in RL refers to:
A) Trading off computational resources for model accuracy
B) Balancing trying new actions to discover better rewards (exploration) vs. using known good actions (exploitation)
C) Trading off training time for inference speed
D) Balancing model complexity against training data size
solution: Exploitation: take the action with highest estimated reward (greedy). Exploration: try less-known actions that might yield higher rewards. Pure exploitation: gets stuck in local optima. Pure exploration: never uses knowledge gained. ε-greedy: with probability ε take random action (explore), otherwise take best known action (exploit). Decreasing ε over time balances exploration in early training with exploitation later.
explanation: Exploration strategies: ε-greedy, Boltzmann/softmax exploration (actions chosen with probability proportional to exp(Q/T)), UCB (Upper Confidence Bound — choose action with highest Q + exploration bonus), Thompson sampling (Bayesian approach). Intrinsic motivation: reward bonus for visiting novel states (count-based, curiosity-driven).

statement:
REINFORCE (vanilla policy gradient) suffers from high variance because:
A) It uses a neural network for the policy
B) The gradient estimate uses the total return of an episode, which has high variance over many steps and random outcomes
C) It requires a large action space
D) It cannot handle continuous action spaces
solution: REINFORCE gradient: ∇J(θ) = E[Σ_t ∇log π_θ(a_t|s_t) · G_t] where G_t = Σ_{k≥t} γ^k r_{k+t} (return from step t). G_t includes all future rewards, which are stochastic — high variance in estimates. This requires many episodes for stable gradient estimates. Solutions: baselines (subtract V(s_t) from G_t to get advantage A_t = G_t - V(s_t)), actor-critic methods.
explanation: Actor-Critic: actor (policy network) + critic (value network). Critic estimates V(s), used to compute advantage A = r + γV(s') - V(s). This reduces variance by replacing noisy Monte Carlo returns with bootstrapped TD estimates. PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization) adds a clipped objective for stable training — widely used for LLM RLHF.

statement:
The Markov property in a Markov Decision Process (MDP) states that:
A) Rewards must be non-negative
B) The future state and reward depend only on the current state and action, not on the history of past states
C) The policy must be deterministic
D) The action space must be finite
solution: Markov property: P(s_{t+1}, r_t | s_t, a_t, s_{t-1}, a_{t-1}, ...) = P(s_{t+1}, r_t | s_t, a_t). The current state contains all relevant history. This enables efficient dynamic programming solutions (value iteration, policy iteration). Without Markov property (POMDP — Partial Observability), we need to maintain beliefs over possible states.
explanation: MDP components: (S, A, P, R, γ). Value function: V^π(s) = E_π[Σγ^t r_t | s_0=s]. Bellman expectation: V^π(s) = Σ_a π(a|s) Σ_{s'} P(s'|s,a)[R(s,a,s') + γV^π(s')]. Solving MDPs: model-based (know P, R) → value/policy iteration. Model-free → Q-learning, policy gradient.

statement: Derive the closed-form ordinary least squares linear regression estimator β_hat = (X^T X)^(-1) X^T y.
answer: The OLS estimator minimizes ||y - Xβ||_2^2. Setting the gradient -2X^T(y-Xβ) to zero yields X^T X β = X^T y, so if X^T X is invertible, β_hat = (X^T X)^(-1)X^T y.
solution: Let J(β)=(y-Xβ)^T(y-Xβ)=y^Ty-2β^TX^Ty+β^TX^TXβ. Differentiating gives ∇βJ=-2X^Ty+2X^TXβ. At the minimizer, X^TXβ=X^Ty. If the columns of X are linearly independent, X^TX is nonsingular and the unique solution is β_hat=(X^TX)^(-1)X^Ty.
explanation: The normal equations express that residuals are orthogonal to every column of X. If X^TX is singular, use a pseudoinverse or regularization.

statement: Explain how the kernel trick lets SVMs solve non-linear classification problems, and define Mercer's theorem.
answer: The kernel trick replaces inner products φ(x_i)^Tφ(x_j) with a kernel K(x_i,x_j), allowing a linear maximum-margin separator in an implicit high-dimensional feature space. Mercer's theorem states that a continuous symmetric positive semidefinite kernel corresponds to an inner product in some feature space.
solution: In the SVM dual, data appear only through dot products. Replacing x_i^Tx_j with K(x_i,x_j) implicitly maps inputs through φ without explicitly constructing φ. Nonlinear kernels such as polynomial and RBF kernels therefore produce nonlinear decision boundaries in input space while keeping optimization in terms of kernel evaluations.
explanation: A valid Mercer kernel has a positive semidefinite Gram matrix for any finite sample, ensuring the SVM optimization remains convex.

statement: Detail the mathematical and structural differences between bagging and boosting, contrasting Random Forests with Gradient Boosting Machines.
answer: Bagging averages independently trained high-variance learners over bootstrap samples to reduce variance; Random Forests add random feature subsampling. Boosting builds learners sequentially so each new tree fits errors or negative gradients of the current ensemble; GBMs reduce bias by additive functional gradient descent.
solution: Random Forest prediction is typically f(x)=average_t h_t(x), where h_t are independent deep trees trained on bootstrap samples and random feature subsets. GBM prediction is f_M(x)=f_0(x)+Σ_m ν h_m(x), where h_m is fit to residuals or negative gradients of a differentiable loss. Bagging parallelizes naturally and stabilizes unstable learners; boosting is sequential and can overfit if learning rate, depth, or iterations are poorly controlled.
explanation: Random Forests mainly decorrelate trees to lower variance. GBMs iteratively improve a weak model and often achieve lower bias but require stronger regularization.

statement: How do L1 (Lasso) and L2 (Ridge) regularization affect weight vectors differently, and why does L1 lead to sparsity?
answer: L2 shrinks weights smoothly toward zero, while L1 applies a constant-magnitude shrinkage that can set coefficients exactly to zero. L1 leads to sparsity because its diamond-shaped constraint has corners aligned with coordinate axes and its penalty is non-differentiable at zero.
solution: Ridge minimizes loss + λΣw_j^2, whose gradient 2λw_j scales with weight size, so small coefficients are gently shrunk. Lasso minimizes loss + λΣ|w_j|, whose subgradient is λ sign(w_j) away from zero and an interval at zero, allowing the optimum to land exactly at w_j=0.
explanation: Geometrically, elliptical loss contours often touch the L1 ball at a corner, producing zero coordinates; the L2 ball is smooth, so exact zeros are uncommon.

statement: In a highly imbalanced classification dataset, why are F1-score or PR AUC better metrics than Accuracy or ROC AUC?
answer: Accuracy can be dominated by the majority class, and ROC AUC can look strong when false-positive rates are small relative to a huge negative class. F1 and PR AUC focus on precision and recall for the positive class, making them more informative when positives are rare.
solution: If only 1% of samples are positive, a classifier that always predicts negative has 99% accuracy but zero recall. Precision-recall curves directly measure how many predicted positives are correct and how many true positives are recovered. ROC curves use FPR=FP/(FP+TN), which can remain deceptively low even when many false alarms occur in absolute terms.
explanation: Use PR AUC when the rare positive class is the main target; use F1 when a single operating threshold and balance between precision and recall are required.

statement: Explain the vanishing gradient problem in deep neural networks and how ResNet skip connections F(x)+x mitigate it.
answer: Vanishing gradients occur when repeated Jacobian products have singular values below one, causing early layers to receive tiny updates. ResNet blocks output y=F(x)+x, giving gradients a direct identity path so ∂L/∂x includes ∂L/∂y in addition to the residual branch.
solution: For many layers, backprop multiplies derivatives through each layer; sigmoid/tanh saturation or poorly scaled weights can make the product shrink exponentially. In a residual block y=F(x)+x, ∂L/∂x=∂L/∂y(I+∂F/∂x). The identity term preserves gradient flow even if the residual branch is small or poorly conditioned.
explanation: Skip connections also make it easier to learn perturbations around identity mappings rather than entirely new transformations.

statement: Detail the mathematical and operational differences between Batch Normalization and Layer Normalization, and when to prefer each.
answer: BatchNorm normalizes each feature/channel using statistics across the mini-batch, while LayerNorm normalizes all features within each sample. BatchNorm is common in CNNs with large stable batches; LayerNorm is preferred in transformers, RNNs, and small-batch or variable-length settings.
solution: BatchNorm computes μ_c and σ_c over batch and spatial positions for each channel, then applies γ_c(x-μ_c)/sqrt(σ_c^2+ε)+β_c and uses running averages at inference. LayerNorm computes μ and σ over a sample's hidden dimensions and uses the same operation during training and inference without batch dependence.
explanation: BatchNorm can improve CNN optimization but is sensitive to batch size and distributed statistics. LayerNorm is stable for sequence models because each token/sample is normalized independently.

statement: What is the role of the KL divergence term in the loss function of a Variational Autoencoder?
answer: The KL term regularizes the encoder's approximate posterior q(z|x) toward the prior p(z), usually N(0,I), making the latent space smooth, continuous, and sampleable.
solution: The VAE maximizes the ELBO: E_q[log p(x|z)] - KL(q(z|x)||p(z)). The reconstruction term encourages z to preserve information about x; the KL term penalizes latent distributions that drift too far from the prior. For Gaussian q, the KL has a closed form involving μ and σ.
explanation: Without the KL term, the model behaves more like a deterministic autoencoder and random prior samples may decode poorly.

statement: How does Adam combine momentum and RMSProp?
answer: Adam maintains an exponential moving average of gradients like momentum and an exponential moving average of squared gradients like RMSProp, then uses bias-corrected estimates to adapt each parameter's step size.
solution: Adam updates m_t=β1m_{t-1}+(1-β1)g_t and v_t=β2v_{t-1}+(1-β2)g_t^2. After bias correction, parameters update as θ_t=θ_{t-1}-α m_hat_t/(sqrt(v_hat_t)+ε). m_t gives directional smoothing; v_t scales down coordinates with consistently large gradients.
explanation: The method is popular because it combines fast initial progress, per-parameter adaptivity, and reduced gradient noise sensitivity.

statement: Explain Dropout during training versus inference. How must weights be scaled during test time if Dropout is used?
answer: Dropout randomly zeros activations during training to prevent co-adaptation. With original dropout, test-time outgoing weights or activations are multiplied by the keep probability p; with inverted dropout, activations are divided by p during training, so no test-time scaling is needed.
solution: During training, mask m_j~Bernoulli(p) and use h'_j=m_jh_j. The expected activation is ph_j, so original dropout compensates at inference by scaling by p. Most modern libraries implement inverted dropout: h'_j=m_jh_j/p, preserving expectation during training and leaving inference unchanged.
explanation: Dropout approximates averaging many subnetworks and improves robustness, but it is often reduced or omitted in architectures already strongly regularized by normalization and data scale.

statement: How does scaled dot-product self-attention calculate weights? Explain Attention(Q,K,V)=softmax(QK^T/sqrt(d_k))V.
answer: Queries are compared to keys by dot product, scaled by sqrt(d_k), normalized with softmax into attention weights, and used to form weighted sums of values.
solution: For each token query q_i, scores s_ij=q_i·k_j/sqrt(d_k) measure compatibility with every key. softmax over j converts scores into probabilities α_ij. The output for token i is Σ_j α_ij v_j. Scaling prevents dot products from growing too large with dimensionality, which would saturate softmax and reduce gradient quality.
explanation: In self-attention, Q, K, and V are learned projections of the same token sequence; multi-head attention repeats this in multiple subspaces.

statement: Contrast Word2Vec CBOW and Skip-gram with modern contextual embeddings like BERT.
answer: CBOW predicts a target word from surrounding words; Skip-gram predicts surrounding words from a target word. Both produce one static vector per word type, while BERT produces contextual token embeddings whose meaning changes with sentence context using bidirectional transformer self-attention.
solution: Word2Vec learns shallow embedding matrices from local co-occurrence objectives. CBOW is faster and smooths over context; Skip-gram performs well for rare words. BERT is pre-trained with masked language modeling and deep transformer layers, so the vector for 'bank' differs in river-bank versus finance-bank contexts.
explanation: Static embeddings are lightweight and useful for simple semantic similarity; contextual embeddings dominate modern NLP because they model syntax, polysemy, and long-range interactions.

statement: What is Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE), and why is it standard for modern LLM tokenization over word-level or character-level tokenization?
answer: BPE starts from characters or bytes and repeatedly merges frequent adjacent symbol pairs to form subword units. It balances vocabulary size and sequence length, handles rare or unseen words, and avoids the huge vocabularies of word-level tokenization and long sequences of character-level tokenization.
solution: Training counts adjacent token pairs in a corpus, merges the most frequent pair, and repeats until a target vocabulary size is reached. Common morphemes and words become single tokens, while rare words decompose into subwords or bytes.
explanation: BPE gives open-vocabulary behavior, efficient computation, and robust handling of names, technical terms, and multilingual text.

statement: Explain the purpose of positional encodings in Transformers and how sine/cosine functions inject sequence order.
answer: Self-attention alone is permutation-invariant, so positional encodings add order information to token embeddings. Sinusoidal encodings use different-frequency sine and cosine waves so each position has a unique vector and relative offsets can be represented linearly.
solution: The original Transformer uses PE(pos,2i)=sin(pos/10000^(2i/d_model)) and PE(pos,2i+1)=cos(pos/10000^(2i/d_model)). These vectors are added to token embeddings before attention, enabling the model to distinguish token positions while preserving parallel computation.
explanation: Modern models may use learned absolute embeddings, RoPE, or ALiBi, but the goal remains to provide sequence-order information.

statement: What is the difference between greedy decoding, beam search, and nucleus (top-p) sampling during text generation?
answer: Greedy decoding always chooses the highest-probability next token; beam search keeps the best k partial sequences; nucleus sampling randomly samples from the smallest token set whose cumulative probability reaches p.
solution: Greedy is fast but can be myopic and repetitive. Beam search explores multiple high-likelihood continuations and is useful for tasks with constrained outputs, but can produce generic text. Nucleus sampling truncates the low-probability tail while preserving stochasticity, making it better for creative open-ended generation.
explanation: Decoding changes how probabilities are used at inference; it does not retrain the model.

statement: How does a convolutional layer compute spatial output dimensions given input size W, filter size F, padding P, and stride S?
answer: The output size is floor((W - F + 2P)/S) + 1 for each spatial dimension.
solution: A filter of size F slides over a padded input of effective size W+2P. The number of valid starting positions separated by stride S is floor((W+2P-F)/S)+1. Apply the same formula independently to height and width.
explanation: If the numerator is not divisible by S, most frameworks floor the result unless explicit output sizing rules are used.

statement: Explain Intersection over Union (IoU) and its role in Non-Maximum Suppression for filtering bounding boxes.
answer: IoU is area(intersection)/area(union) between two boxes. In NMS, boxes are sorted by confidence, the best box is kept, and lower-scoring boxes with IoU above a threshold are suppressed as duplicates.
solution: IoU ranges from 0 for no overlap to 1 for identical boxes. NMS iteratively selects the highest-confidence remaining detection and removes nearby detections that overlap too much, usually class-wise. This turns many candidate boxes around the same object into one final prediction.
explanation: A low NMS threshold removes duplicates aggressively but may suppress crowded objects; a high threshold preserves crowded objects but may leave duplicates.

statement: Contrast U-Net and Mask R-CNN architectural designs and primary image segmentation use cases.
answer: U-Net is an encoder-decoder with skip connections for dense semantic segmentation, especially biomedical or pixel-wise prediction. Mask R-CNN is a two-stage detector that adds a mask head to Faster R-CNN for instance segmentation of individual objects.
solution: U-Net downsamples to capture context and upsamples while concatenating high-resolution encoder features for precise boundaries. It outputs per-pixel class maps. Mask R-CNN proposes regions, classifies boxes, refines bounding boxes, and predicts a separate binary mask for each detected instance.
explanation: Use U-Net when every pixel needs a class label; use Mask R-CNN when separating individual object instances matters.

statement: What is Mixup data augmentation, and how does interpolating images and labels improve robustness?
answer: Mixup creates synthetic samples x'=λx_i+(1-λ)x_j and soft labels y'=λy_i+(1-λ)y_j. It encourages linear behavior between examples, reduces memorization, and improves calibration and robustness.
solution: λ is usually sampled from a Beta distribution. Because labels are mixed with inputs, the model is not forced into overconfident one-hot predictions for ambiguous interpolated samples. This smooths decision boundaries and acts as data-dependent regularization.
explanation: Mixup is especially helpful when labels are noisy or datasets are small, though it can be less natural for tasks requiring precise localization unless adapted.

statement: How does a Vision Transformer patchify an image, and how does it differ from a CNN in extracting local versus global features?
answer: A ViT splits an image into fixed-size patches, flattens and linearly projects each patch into a token, adds positional information, and applies transformer self-attention. CNNs use local convolutional kernels with strong locality and translation biases; ViTs model global patch interactions directly but need more data or pretraining.
solution: For an H×W image with P×P patches, ViT forms N=HW/P^2 tokens. Self-attention can connect every patch to every other patch in a layer. CNN receptive fields grow gradually through stacked local filters and pooling.
explanation: CNNs are sample-efficient for local visual patterns; ViTs are flexible global sequence models but have quadratic attention cost in token count.

statement: Derive the MLE for the variance of a Gaussian distribution and explain why it is biased.
answer: For Gaussian samples with unknown mean, the MLE is σ_hat^2=(1/n)Σ(x_i-x_bar)^2. It is biased downward because E[Σ(x_i-x_bar)^2]=(n-1)σ^2, so E[σ_hat^2]=((n-1)/n)σ^2.
solution: Maximizing the Gaussian log-likelihood over μ gives μ_hat=x_bar. Differentiating with respect to σ^2 and setting to zero gives σ_hat^2=(1/n)Σ(x_i-x_bar)^2. Since estimating μ consumes one degree of freedom, the expected sum of squared deviations is (n-1)σ^2.
explanation: The unbiased sample variance divides by n-1, not n. The MLE is still consistent because the bias vanishes as n grows.

statement: What is the difference between Type I and Type II errors, and how does statistical power relate to them?
answer: A Type I error rejects a true null hypothesis; a Type II error fails to reject a false null hypothesis. Power is 1 minus the Type II error probability, the chance of correctly detecting a real effect.
solution: If α=P(reject H0 | H0 true), α is the Type I error rate. If β=P(fail to reject H0 | H1 true), β is the Type II error rate. Power=1-β increases with larger sample size, larger effect size, lower noise, and sometimes a higher α threshold.
explanation: Designing a test requires balancing false positives, false negatives, sample size, and the practical cost of each error.

statement: Explain Markov Chain Monte Carlo and describe the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm.
answer: MCMC constructs a Markov chain whose stationary distribution is the target posterior. Metropolis-Hastings proposes a new state, accepts it with a probability correcting for target density and proposal asymmetry, and otherwise stays at the current state.
solution: At state x, sample proposal x'~q(x'|x). Accept with probability min(1, [π(x')q(x|x')]/[π(x)q(x'|x)]). If accepted set x=x'; otherwise retain x. After burn-in, retained samples approximate expectations under π.
explanation: MCMC is useful when direct posterior normalization is intractable but unnormalized density values can be evaluated.

statement: Explain the Central Limit Theorem. Does it apply to distributions with infinite variance such as the Cauchy distribution?
answer: The classical CLT says normalized sums of i.i.d. variables with finite mean and variance converge in distribution to a Gaussian. It does not apply to Cauchy variables because the Cauchy has no finite mean or variance; averages of Cauchy samples remain Cauchy-distributed.
solution: For i.i.d. X_i with mean μ and variance σ^2<∞, sqrt(n)(X_bar-μ)/σ converges to N(0,1). Infinite-variance distributions require generalized stable-law results, not the standard Gaussian CLT.
explanation: Heavy tails can make sample means unstable, so robust statistics such as medians may be more meaningful.

statement: What is the difference between Pearson correlation and Spearman rank correlation, and when choose Spearman?
answer: Pearson measures linear association between raw numeric variables; Spearman measures monotonic association between ranks. Choose Spearman for ordinal data, monotonic nonlinear relationships, heavy outliers, or non-normal variables.
solution: Pearson is covariance divided by the product of standard deviations. Spearman first replaces values by ranks and then computes Pearson correlation on those ranks. Ranking makes it less sensitive to scale and extreme values.
explanation: If the relationship is curved but consistently increasing or decreasing, Spearman can be high while Pearson may underestimate association.

statement: Task 1: Adversarial Attacks on CNNs. Generate adversarial examples to systematically fool a pre-trained ResNet image classifier and reduce validation accuracy below 10% while minimizing perturbation epsilon.
answer: Implement FGSM or PGD by enabling gradients on input pixels, maximizing classification loss with respect to the image, clipping perturbations to an epsilon ball, and measuring attacked accuracy.
solution: Load the pre-trained model and validation images, normalize inputs consistently, set x.requires_grad=True, compute cross-entropy, backpropagate to x.grad, and update x_adv using sign gradients. PGD repeats small steps with projection into ||x_adv-x||_∞≤ε and valid pixel ranges. Sweep ε to find the smallest value that drops accuracy below 10%.
explanation: Unlike training, the model weights stay fixed; the optimization variable is the input image.

statement: Task 2: Semantic Changes in Word Embeddings. Train Word2Vec embeddings on 1950s and 2020s corpora, align vector spaces with Orthogonal Procrustes, and output the top 50 words with largest cosine distance shifts.
answer: Train comparable embeddings, restrict to shared vocabulary anchor words, solve R*=argmin_R ||XR-Y||_F with R orthogonal, transform one space, and rank common words by cosine distance.
solution: Use identical preprocessing and Word2Vec hyperparameters for both corpora. Build matrices X and Y for shared stable anchor vocabulary, compute SVD of X^TY=UΣV^T, set R=UV^T, align X' = XR, then compute 1-cosine_similarity(X'_w,Y_w) for each common word and return the largest distances.
explanation: Procrustes alignment removes arbitrary rotations from independently trained embedding spaces while preserving distances within each space.

statement: Task 3: Multispectral Segmentation / Coin Counting Machine. Build a CV pipeline to detect coin bounding boxes, classify denominations, and output total monetary sum from top-down images.
answer: Parse COCO or YOLO annotations, fine-tune a detector such as YOLOv8 or Faster R-CNN, apply confidence thresholding and customized NMS, classify denomination per detection, and sum detected values.
solution: Prepare train/validation splits, convert annotations to the detector format, fine-tune with augmentations suited to circles and lighting, evaluate mAP and counting error, then post-process detections with class-aware NMS tuned for overlapping coins. The final pipeline maps each class to a denomination and returns Σ count_class × value_class.
explanation: The key challenge is balancing duplicate suppression against missed detections in dense overlapping scenes.

statement: In a system using over 200 distinct tool calls, how does a hierarchical agent architecture minimize compounding error compared with a flat routing structure?
answer: Hierarchy decomposes routing into smaller decisions with scoped specialists, local validation, and escalation paths, reducing the effective branching factor and isolating errors before they propagate through the whole tool chain.
solution: A flat router must choose among hundreds of tools at each step, so even a small per-decision error can compound across long trajectories. A hierarchical router first selects a domain or sub-agent, then that sub-agent chooses from a smaller tool set with domain-specific prompts, memory, and checks. Supervisors can verify outputs, retry failed subtasks, and aggregate only validated results.
explanation: The architecture trades some latency for lower routing entropy, better observability, and fault containment.

statement: When predicting crop yields from tabular meteorological data, how do you handle high-cardinality categorical features without target leakage?
answer: Use leakage-safe encodings such as out-of-fold target encoding, frequency/count encoding, hashing, learned embeddings, or CatBoost-style ordered statistics, always fitting encoders only on training folds and applying them to validation/test data.
solution: For target encoding, split training data into folds. For each fold, compute category means using only the other folds, smooth toward the global mean, and encode the held-out fold. For test data, compute encodings from the full training set only. Group or time-aware splits are required if locations or seasons repeat.
explanation: Computing category target means on the same rows being evaluated leaks label information and inflates validation performance.

statement: When securing backend endpoints, what unsupervised algorithms best detect irregular access patterns resembling a JWT forgery attempt before authentication layers fail?
answer: Useful methods include Isolation Forest, One-Class SVM, Local Outlier Factor, robust covariance models, autoencoders, and sequence models over request behavior. Features should capture token metadata anomalies, endpoint transitions, timing, IP/device changes, and privilege-use patterns.
solution: Isolation Forest scales well for tabular request features and detects rare combinations. LOF identifies locally unusual traffic. Autoencoders learn normal multivariate patterns and flag high reconstruction error. For ordered endpoint calls, HMMs or recurrent/transformer autoencoders can model abnormal sequences before hard authentication failures occur.
explanation: These systems should complement, not replace, cryptographic JWT verification and standard authentication controls.

statement: Formulate the Bellman optimality equation V(s)=max_a(R(s,a)+γΣ_{s'}P(s'|s,a)V(s')) and explain its role in training a routing agent.
answer: The Bellman equation defines the optimal value of a state as the best immediate reward plus discounted expected future value. A routing agent uses it to choose the action or tool route with maximum long-term utility, not just immediate success.
solution: For state s describing the current task and context, action a may select a tool or sub-agent. R(s,a) scores immediate benefit such as correctness, cost, or latency. P(s'|s,a) models possible next states. The value function is updated until it satisfies the Bellman fixed point, yielding policy π*(s)=argmax_a[R(s,a)+γΣP(s'|s,a)V(s')].
explanation: This supports planning under uncertainty when a route may be costly now but improves downstream task completion.

statement: How does t-SNE differ from PCA when preserving local versus global structure in high-dimensional agent state logs?
answer: PCA is a linear projection preserving directions of maximum global variance; t-SNE is a nonlinear embedding designed to preserve local neighborhoods and clusters, often at the expense of global distances and cluster sizes.
solution: PCA computes orthogonal components from the covariance matrix and is deterministic, fast, and interpretable. t-SNE converts pairwise distances into neighborhood probabilities and optimizes a low-dimensional map whose probabilities match, using a heavy-tailed distribution to separate clusters.
explanation: Use PCA for compression, denoising, and global trends; use t-SNE mainly for visualization of local structure, not quantitative distance analysis.

statement: Explain the mathematical intuition behind BFGS and why it is a quasi-Newton method.
answer: BFGS approximates Newton's method by iteratively updating an inverse Hessian estimate from gradient differences instead of computing the true Hessian. It is quasi-Newton because it uses curvature approximations satisfying secant conditions.
solution: Newton uses θ_{k+1}=θ_k-H^{-1}∇f(θ_k). BFGS maintains B_k or H_k≈∇²f^{-1}; after step s_k=θ_{k+1}-θ_k and gradient change y_k=∇f_{k+1}-∇f_k, it updates the matrix so H_{k+1}y_k=s_k while preserving symmetry and positive definiteness under standard conditions.
explanation: BFGS often converges faster than first-order methods on smooth problems but is more memory-intensive; L-BFGS stores only a few curvature pairs.

statement: When can Naive Bayes outperform Logistic Regression despite its conditional independence assumption?
answer: Naive Bayes can outperform Logistic Regression with small datasets, high-dimensional sparse features, strong class-conditional word signals, or when fast online training is needed, because its generative parameter estimates have low variance.
solution: In text classification, word counts can be extremely sparse and dimensional. Naive Bayes estimates P(feature|class) and P(class), needing relatively little data and tolerating many irrelevant features. Logistic Regression is discriminative and often wins with enough labeled data, but it may overfit or require stronger regularization in small-data regimes.
explanation: The independence assumption is often false, but the resulting decision boundary can still be effective for classification.

statement: What architectural modifications to self-attention enable deep reasoning step generation prior to yielding a final output token?
answer: There is no single mandatory self-attention modification that creates reasoning; modern systems usually rely on transformer depth, recurrence or iterative refinement, scratchpad/deliberation tokens, tool use, training objectives, and inference-time compute allocation rather than a fundamentally different attention formula.
solution: Architectural variants may add recurrent memory, latent reasoning tokens, adaptive computation, external memory, or separate planner/verifier modules. Standard causal self-attention can already condition later tokens on earlier generated reasoning tokens; training and decoding policies determine whether the model emits or internally uses intermediate steps before the final answer.
explanation: Claims about proprietary reasoning-model internals should be treated cautiously unless documented; behavior often emerges from data, objectives, and inference procedures.

statement: When using a Llama vision model for plant pathology analysis, how are raw image patches mapped and aligned into the textual token embedding space?
answer: A vision encoder converts image patches into visual embeddings, and a learned projector maps those embeddings to the language model's hidden dimension so they can be inserted as visual tokens alongside text tokens.
solution: The image is resized and patchified, typically by a ViT-like encoder. Patch embeddings pass through transformer layers to produce visual features. A multimodal adapter or projection MLP maps features into the same dimensional space as text embeddings. During instruction tuning, cross-modal objectives teach the language model to attend to visual tokens and produce text diagnoses.
explanation: The exact architecture varies by model family, but patch encoding plus learned projection into the LLM token space is the common pattern.

statement: Derive the gradient of binary cross-entropy L=-[y log(y_hat)+(1-y)log(1-y_hat)] with respect to output layer weights.
answer: For sigmoid output y_hat=σ(z), z=w^Tx+b, the gradient is ∂L/∂w=(y_hat-y)x and ∂L/∂b=y_hat-y.
solution: First ∂L/∂y_hat= -y/y_hat + (1-y)/(1-y_hat). For sigmoid, ∂y_hat/∂z=y_hat(1-y_hat). Multiplying simplifies to ∂L/∂z=y_hat-y. Since ∂z/∂w=x, ∂L/∂w=(y_hat-y)x.
explanation: This simplification is why sigmoid plus BCE is numerically and mathematically convenient for binary classification.

statement: Explain how temporal awareness is achieved in modern autoregressive models using Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE).
answer: RoPE injects position by rotating query and key vectors in paired dimensions by angles depending on token position, making attention scores depend naturally on relative positions.
solution: For each position p and frequency θ_i, RoPE applies a 2D rotation to pairs of query/key coordinates. The dot product between a rotated query at position m and key at position n depends on m-n, giving relative temporal information without adding separate position vectors to values.
explanation: RoPE is widely used because it encodes order inside attention and can extrapolate better than some learned absolute embeddings, though long-context scaling often needs additional techniques.

statement: Contrast the computational cost and effectiveness of contrastive decoding versus strict temperature scaling for reducing hallucinations in an advisory chatbot.
answer: Temperature scaling is cheap because it only rescales logits, but it mainly reduces randomness. Contrastive decoding is costlier because it compares distributions from stronger/weaker models or alternative contexts, but it can more directly penalize generic or unsupported continuations.
solution: Lower temperature concentrates probability mass on high-likelihood tokens and may reduce bizarre outputs, but it cannot add missing evidence. Contrastive decoding scores tokens using a main model minus a penalty from an amateur model or undesirable distribution, often requiring extra forward passes and careful tuning.
explanation: For factual advisory systems, decoding controls should be combined with retrieval, citation checks, refusal policies, and verification.

statement: Why is He initialization preferred over Xavier initialization for networks using ReLU activations?
answer: ReLU zeroes roughly half of activations, so He initialization uses variance 2/fan_in to preserve activation and gradient variance. Xavier assumes more symmetric activations and typically uses variance near 1/fan_in or 2/(fan_in+fan_out).
solution: For stable deep networks, signal variance should not explode or vanish layer by layer. Because ReLU passes only the positive half of a zero-centered input, the variance is reduced; He initialization compensates with a larger weight variance.
explanation: Xavier is better matched to tanh/sigmoid-like activations, while He is designed for ReLU and variants.

statement: How does a Sparse Autoencoder enforce sparsity in hidden representations, and what mathematical penalty is added to the loss?
answer: A sparse autoencoder penalizes hidden units for being active too often, commonly with an L1 activation penalty or a KL divergence between desired sparsity ρ and average activation ρ_hat_j.
solution: The loss can be reconstruction_loss + λΣ_j |h_j| for L1 sparsity, or reconstruction_loss + βΣ_j KL(ρ||ρ_hat_j), where KL(ρ||ρ_hat)=ρ log(ρ/ρ_hat)+(1-ρ)log((1-ρ)/(1-ρ_hat)). This encourages most hidden activations to be near zero.
explanation: Sparsity can produce more interpretable, parts-based features and reduce overcomplete memorization.

statement: Design a system prompt architecture that establishes an immutable semantic sandbox to prevent jailbreaks in a public-facing language API.
answer: Use layered instructions with non-overridable system policies, strict tool schemas, input/output validation, retrieval isolation, least-privilege tools, explicit refusal rules, and monitoring; no prompt alone is truly immutable against all attacks.
solution: Separate developer policy from user content with delimiters and metadata, classify untrusted text as data, prohibit following instructions found in retrieved/user documents, enforce allowlisted tool calls, require citations for RAG claims, and run post-generation policy checks. Store secrets outside prompts and never expose credentials to the model context.
explanation: Security must be implemented as defense-in-depth in the application, not only as natural-language prompt wording.

statement: In Retrieval-Augmented Generation, how does hybrid search combining BM25 with vector similarity improve recall for specific domain terminology?
answer: BM25 captures exact lexical matches for rare terms, acronyms, IDs, and formulas, while vector search captures semantic paraphrases. Combining them improves recall when either exact wording or semantic similarity alone would miss relevant documents.
solution: Hybrid systems retrieve candidates from both sparse BM25 and dense embeddings, then merge or re-rank them, often with a cross-encoder. This helps domain queries such as chemical names, legal citations, crop disease names, or API error codes where exact tokens matter.
explanation: Dense embeddings may blur rare specialized terms; BM25 may miss synonyms. Hybrid retrieval covers both failure modes.

statement: Calculate BPE merge operations given a predefined frequency dictionary of character sequences.
answer: At each step, count adjacent symbol-pair frequencies weighted by word frequency, merge the most frequent pair, update the vocabulary sequences, and repeat until the requested number of merges or vocabulary size is reached.
solution: For example, if low:5, lower:2, newest:6, widest:3 are split into characters plus end markers, compute counts such as (l,o), (o,w), and so on weighted by frequencies. Merge the highest-count pair, replace every occurrence of that adjacent pair, then recompute counts for the next merge.
explanation: A concrete numeric answer depends on the supplied frequency dictionary and requested merge count; deterministic tie-breaking should be specified.

statement: How does speculative decoding accelerate LLM inference without changing the final output probability distribution?
answer: A smaller draft model proposes multiple tokens, and the larger target model verifies them in parallel with an accept/reject rule that preserves the target model's distribution exactly.
solution: The draft model samples a candidate block quickly. The target model evaluates probabilities for all proposed positions in one forward pass. Tokens are accepted when they are consistent with target probabilities; rejected positions are resampled from a corrected distribution. Because acceptance is mathematically adjusted, outputs match sampling from the target model.
explanation: Speedups occur when the draft model often predicts tokens the target model would likely accept, reducing sequential target-model calls.

statement: Why is ROUGE criticized for abstractive summarization, and how do model-based metrics like BERTScore address these flaws?
answer: ROUGE measures n-gram overlap, so it can penalize valid paraphrases and reward lexical copying. BERTScore compares contextual embeddings, capturing more semantic similarity between generated and reference summaries.
solution: Abstractive summaries may use different wording while preserving meaning. ROUGE-L and n-gram ROUGE miss many synonym and entailment relationships. BERTScore aligns tokens in embedding space and computes precision/recall/F1 over semantic similarities, making it less dependent on exact wording.
explanation: Model-based metrics are not perfect; they can inherit biases and may still miss factual consistency, so human or factuality evaluation remains important.

statement: Detail the Transformer FFN sub-layer: FFN(x)=max(0,xW1+b1)W2+b2.
answer: The FFN is a position-wise two-layer MLP applied independently to each token: expand hidden dimension, apply nonlinearity, then project back to model dimension.
solution: For each token vector x, W1 maps d_model to d_ff, ReLU or a modern activation such as GELU/SwiGLU adds nonlinearity, and W2 maps d_ff back to d_model. The same FFN weights are shared across sequence positions but not across layers.
explanation: Attention mixes information across tokens; the FFN performs nonlinear feature transformation within each token representation.

statement: Explain channel fusion when feeding 7-channel multispectral satellite imagery into a standard U-Net.
answer: Modify the first convolution to accept 7 channels, or use a learned 1x1/stem projection to fuse spectral bands into the feature dimension expected by U-Net. Normalize each band separately and preserve geospatial alignment.
solution: If the original U-Net expects RGB, replace Conv2d(in_channels=3,...) with Conv2d(in_channels=7,...). For pretrained RGB weights, initialize extra channels by averaging RGB filters, random initialization, or a spectral adapter. Early fusion stacks all bands; late fusion uses separate encoders for band groups and merges features later.
explanation: The best fusion strategy depends on band semantics, data volume, and whether pretrained RGB weights are valuable.

statement: For mobile leaf anomaly detection, what are the trade-offs of MobileNetV3 versus ResNet50 regarding FLOPs and memory bandwidth?
answer: MobileNetV3 uses depthwise separable convolutions, squeeze-and-excitation, and lightweight blocks to greatly reduce parameters and FLOPs versus ResNet50, improving mobile latency and memory use, but it may have lower accuracy or robustness on complex pathology patterns.
solution: ResNet50 uses many dense convolutions with high channel counts, giving strong representation capacity but higher compute and activation memory. MobileNetV3 factorizes convolution into depthwise and pointwise operations, reducing arithmetic but sometimes becoming memory-bandwidth-bound because depthwise convolutions have lower arithmetic intensity.
explanation: Choose MobileNetV3 for edge deployment constraints; choose ResNet50 or a larger model when server inference or maximum accuracy is more important.

statement: Describe frequency-domain artifacts CNNs use to distinguish real photos from GAN-generated images.
answer: Detectors may exploit abnormal high-frequency spectra, checkerboard upsampling artifacts, periodic texture patterns, sensor-noise inconsistencies, and missing camera processing fingerprints.
solution: Generative models can leave frequency peaks or unnatural correlations from transposed convolutions, resizing, denoising, or decoder architectures. Applying DCT/FFT or high-pass filters can expose artifacts that are subtle in RGB space. CNNs can learn filters that detect these spectral irregularities.
explanation: Artifact-based detectors can fail under compression, resizing, or new generators, so robust evaluation across sources is necessary.

statement: How is the Kalman filter used to predict future bounding boxes in DeepSORT?
answer: DeepSORT represents each track with a motion state including box center, aspect ratio, height, and velocities. A Kalman filter predicts the next state, then updates it with matched detector measurements.
solution: The prediction step applies a linear motion model x_t=Fx_{t-1}+noise and updates covariance. Detections are associated to predicted tracks using motion gating plus appearance embeddings. Once a detection is matched, the Kalman update corrects the state and reduces uncertainty.
explanation: The Kalman filter bridges missed detections and provides geometrically plausible track continuity.

statement: How does Swin Transformer achieve linear computational complexity relative to image size compared with quadratic standard ViT attention?
answer: Swin restricts self-attention to local non-overlapping windows, making attention cost proportional to the number of windows times window area squared. With fixed window size, this scales linearly with image size; shifted windows allow cross-window communication.
solution: Standard ViT attention over N patches costs O(N^2). Swin partitions patches into windows of M tokens and computes attention within each window, costing O((N/M)M^2)=O(NM). Since M is fixed, complexity is O(N). Alternating shifted-window layers exchange information across neighboring windows.
explanation: Swin also uses hierarchical patch merging, making it more CNN-like and suitable for dense vision tasks.

statement: Explain the camera projection matrix P=K[R|t] used to map 3D world coordinates to 2D image coordinates.
answer: [R|t] transforms a 3D world point into camera coordinates, and K applies camera intrinsics to project it onto pixel coordinates in homogeneous form.
solution: For homogeneous world point X_w, compute x~ = K[R|t]X_w. R is rotation, t is translation, and K contains focal lengths and principal point. Pixel coordinates are obtained by perspective division: u=x~/z~, v=y~/z~.
explanation: Extrinsics define camera pose; intrinsics define the camera's internal geometry.

statement: Design an RCT to test whether a new JWT authentication flow significantly increases successful API calls versus legacy validation.
answer: Randomly assign comparable traffic or users to legacy control and new JWT treatment, define success rate as the primary metric, pre-register hypotheses, run a power analysis, and compare proportions with confidence intervals and an appropriate test.
solution: H0: p_new≤p_legacy; H1: p_new>p_legacy. Randomize by user or tenant to avoid cross-contamination, stratify by endpoint or traffic class, monitor latency and security failures as guardrails, and analyze with a two-proportion z-test or logistic regression with covariates. Use intention-to-treat analysis and stop according to a pre-defined plan.
explanation: The experiment should measure reliability without weakening security checks or exposing users to unacceptable risk.

statement: For missing points in periodic physical systems such as pendulum motion, why can spline interpolation be superior to linear interpolation?
answer: Splines produce smooth curves with continuous derivatives, better matching physical trajectories with velocity and acceleration continuity, whereas linear interpolation creates sharp corners and piecewise-constant velocity.
solution: Cubic splines fit piecewise cubic polynomials constrained to match values and derivative smoothness at knots. For pendulum-like motion sampled sufficiently densely, this better approximates curved dynamics between observations. Periodic splines can additionally enforce matching endpoints over cycles.
explanation: Splines can overshoot or fail with large gaps; physics-informed models may be better when governing equations are known.

statement: Agent A succeeds with probability 0.95 and Agent B with 0.90. If they operate independently in parallel and only one needs to succeed, calculate overall success probability.
solution: Overall failure occurs only if both fail. P(both fail)=0.05×0.10=0.005 under independence. Therefore P(at least one succeeds)=1-0.005=0.995.
explanation: If the agents' failures are correlated, this independence calculation would overestimate reliability.

statement: Explain the Poisson distribution and its application to modeling asynchronous tool request arrivals at a server.
answer: The Poisson distribution models counts of independent events in a fixed interval with constant average rate λ. It can model the number of asynchronous tool requests arriving per second or minute when arrivals are approximately independent and stationary.
solution: P(N=k)=e^{-λ}λ^k/k!, with mean and variance both equal to λ. In server modeling, λ is the expected arrival count per time window. The related exponential distribution models inter-arrival times in a homogeneous Poisson process.
explanation: Real traffic may be bursty or time-varying, requiring non-homogeneous Poisson, overdispersed, or queueing models.

statement: Prove that Var(X+Y)=Var(X)+Var(Y) for independent random variables X and Y.
answer: Var(X+Y)=Var(X)+Var(Y)+2Cov(X,Y). Independence implies Cov(X,Y)=0, so Var(X+Y)=Var(X)+Var(Y).
solution: Var(X+Y)=E[(X+Y)^2]-[E(X+Y)]^2 = E[X^2]+2E[XY]+E[Y^2]-(E[X]+E[Y])^2. Independence gives E[XY]=E[X]E[Y], so cross terms cancel, leaving E[X^2]-E[X]^2 + E[Y^2]-E[Y]^2.
explanation: Uncorrelated variables also satisfy the same result, but independence is a stronger sufficient condition.

statement: Describe Gibbs sampling as a specific case of Metropolis-Hastings for multivariate distributions.
answer: Gibbs sampling iteratively samples each variable from its full conditional distribution given all others. It is a Metropolis-Hastings special case where the proposal is the exact conditional, so the acceptance probability is 1.
solution: For variables x=(x1,...,xd), update x_j ~ p(x_j | x_-j) for j=1,...,d, repeatedly. Because each proposal is drawn from the target conditional distribution, detailed balance holds without rejection. This constructs a Markov chain with the joint posterior as stationary distribution.
explanation: Gibbs is efficient when full conditionals are easy to sample but can mix slowly when variables are highly correlated.

statement: Task 5: Real or Fake Image Detection. Build a classifier for a 10:1 imbalanced generated-versus-real image dataset that maximizes F1 and explicitly leverages high-frequency noise analysis.

statement: Question 1. 1. Assume a model for medical diagnosis uses accuracy for evaluation. Given that only 5% of patients have a rare disease, accuracy is problematic. (a) Give a general explanation why. (b) Give a specific case for the medical diagnosis model that demonstrates this. 2. Consider a spam email detection system where only 1% of emails are spam. (a) Which evaluation metric is the best choice among precision, recall, and F1-score? (b) Explain the benefits of the best metric. (c) Criticize the remaining metrics.
answer: 1(a) Accuracy is misleading on imbalanced datasets because a model can obtain high accuracy by predicting only the majority class. 1(b) If only 5% of patients have the disease, a model that always predicts 'no disease' achieves 95% accuracy but detects no sick patients. 2(a) F1-score. 2(b) F1 balances precision and recall, so it accounts for both false positives and false negatives when spam is rare. 2(c) Precision alone can ignore missed spam, while recall alone can ignore false alarms; either can give an incomplete picture under severe class imbalance.
solution: For the rare-disease model, let 1000 patients contain 50 disease-positive and 950 disease-negative cases. A trivial classifier that predicts every patient as negative obtains 950/1000 = 95% accuracy, yet recall for the disease class is 0/50 = 0. This shows that accuracy measures majority-class dominance rather than diagnostic usefulness. For spam detection with 1% spam, F1 = 2PR/(P+R) combines precision P = TP/(TP+FP) and recall R = TP/(TP+FN). It is preferred because a useful spam detector should catch spam while avoiding excessive false positives on legitimate mail. Precision alone can be high for a model that flags only a few obvious spam messages but misses most spam. Recall alone can be high for a model that sends too many legitimate emails to spam. F1 penalizes both failure modes.
explanation: The central issue is class imbalance: the majority class dominates accuracy, while minority-class detection quality is better captured by precision, recall, F1, and PR-focused metrics.

statement: Question 2. Select all good answers. 1. A trolley is heading toward a mystery bus with a 50% chance of containing two people. You can pull the lever to divert it to another track, hitting a mystery bus with a 10% chance of 10 people. What should you do? A Pull because it saves more lives. B Do not pull because it saves more lives. C Neither option saves more lives. D It is a moral dilemma and should not be solved only with a probability equation. 2. A job-screening AI favors one socioeconomic background due to historical data. The company must: A ignore the bias; B adjust the AI to remove bias; C collect diverse data and retrain; D combine adjustments and retraining while considering cost/time. 3. In an unavoidable self-driving-car accident choosing between an elderly pedestrian and a young child, the AI should decide by: A hit the elderly pedestrian considering remaining lifespan; B hit the child considering faster recovery; C follow programmed ethical guidelines minimizing overall harm; D make a random decision to avoid bias. 4. A hospital AI is less accurate for women due to male-biased training data. Addressing this requires: A algorithm adjustments; B balanced retraining data; C combination of retraining and adjustments; D continue using because it works for men. 5. AI surveillance disproportionately targets racial or ethnic groups. The city should: A modify AI to eliminate bias; B implement oversight; C keep as is because it reflects crime data; D combine modifications and oversight. 6. A social media recommender is suspected of promoting political views. The company could: A not disclose to protect proprietary information; B disclose fully; C partially disclose; D conduct independent audits instead of full disclosure. 7. Possible ethical resolutions for copyrighted AI training data: A only explicitly free-to-use data; B negotiate agreements with owners; C track and credit creators; D limit training to non-commercial sources.
solution: 1. Expected harm without pulling is 0.5×2 + 0.5×0 = 1 person. Expected harm after pulling is 0.1×10 + 0.9×0 = 1 person. Since the expected values are equal, neither option saves more expected lives; ethical considerations beyond probability may matter, so C and D are good answers. 2. Historical bias should not be ignored. Bias mitigation may require model adjustment, new diverse data, retraining, and practical trade-off analysis, so B, C, and D are good. 3. The supplied answer key accepts A, C, and D: ethical guidelines minimizing harm are central, randomization may be considered to avoid some forms of explicit bias, and remaining lifespan appears as one accepted consideration in this exam key. 4. Male-biased medical data should be addressed by algorithmic adjustment, balanced retraining, or both; continuing unchanged compromises women's health. 5. Discriminatory surveillance should be modified and overseen, preferably with both fairness and resource trade-offs considered. 6. Transparency can be improved through full disclosure, partial disclosure, or independent audits; total secrecy risks public distrust. 7. Ethical copyright approaches include using free-to-use data, licensing or agreements, and creator tracking/crediting. Limiting only to non-commercial sources is not sufficient as a general resolution.
explanation: The question emphasizes selecting every acceptable ethical response, including trade-off-aware combinations rather than single technical fixes.

statement: Question 3. Consider the 2D dataset: #1 (1.90,0.97), #2 (1.76,0.84), #3 (2.32,1.63), #4 (2.31,2.09), #5 (1.14,2.11), #6 (5.02,3.02), #7 (5.74,3.84), #8 (2.25,3.47), #9 (4.71,3.60), #10 (3.17,4.96). Initial k-means centers are θA,0=(1.90,0.97) and θB,0=(3.17,4.96), k=2, Euclidean distance. 1. Simulate the cluster assignment step and give each point's assigned cluster and distance from its nearer initial center. 2. Compute new centers θA,1 and θB,1 from that assignment. 3. Can k-means revisit a configuration? Justify why this proves finite convergence.
answer: Assignments: points 1-5 belong to cluster A and points 6-10 belong to cluster B. Nearest-center distances are: #1 0, #2 0.191, #3 0.7823, #4 1.1929, #5 1.37011, #6 2.68069, #7 2.80344, #8 1.75114, #9 2.05456, #10 0. New centers: θA,1=(1.886,1.528), θB,1=(4.178,3.778). K-means cannot revisit a changed configuration because the objective monotonically decreases whenever the partition changes, and there are finitely many partitions.
solution: Distance is sqrt((x-x_center)^2+(y-y_center)^2). Comparing distances to θA,0 and θB,0 gives cluster A for points 1,2,3,4,5 and cluster B for points 6,7,8,9,10. The nearest distances are: d1=0; d2=sqrt((1.76-1.90)^2+(0.84-0.97)^2)=0.191; d3=sqrt((2.32-1.90)^2+(1.63-0.97)^2)=0.7823; d4=sqrt((2.31-1.90)^2+(2.09-0.97)^2)=1.1929; d5=sqrt((1.14-1.90)^2+(2.11-0.97)^2)=1.37011; d6=sqrt((5.02-3.17)^2+(3.02-4.96)^2)=2.68069; d7=sqrt((5.74-3.17)^2+(3.84-4.96)^2)=2.80344; d8=sqrt((2.25-3.17)^2+(3.47-4.96)^2)=1.75114; d9=sqrt((4.71-3.17)^2+(3.60-4.96)^2)=2.05456; d10=0. The new A center is ((1.90+1.76+2.32+2.31+1.14)/5, (0.97+0.84+1.63+2.09+2.11)/5)=(1.886,1.528). The new B center is ((5.02+5.74+2.25+4.71+3.17)/5, (3.02+3.84+3.47+3.60+4.96)/5)=(4.178,3.778). K-means alternates between assigning points to nearest centers and recomputing means; each nontrivial iteration decreases the within-cluster sum of squared errors. Since only finitely many k-way partitions exist, it cannot keep changing forever or revisit an earlier higher-cost configuration, so it converges in finite steps.
explanation: The convergence argument relies on a finite configuration space and monotonic decrease of the k-means objective, not on convexity of the global problem.

statement: Question 4. DALL-E uses a discrete VAE to encode images into tokens and generates images from these tokens using a Transformer. Suppose the vocabulary has V=8192 discrete tokens and each token embedding has dimensionality d=512. 1. Calculate the number of parameters in the token embedding matrix. 2. A Transformer feed-forward network has two linear transformations: d to f=2048 and f back to d. Compute the total number of parameters for the feed-forward network in one Transformer layer, ignoring biases.
answer: 1. Embedding matrix parameters: V×d = 8192×512 = 4,194,304. 2. FFN parameters: d×f + f×d = 512×2048 + 2048×512 = 1,048,576 + 1,048,576 = 2,097,152, ignoring biases.
solution: The embedding table stores one vector of length 512 for each of 8192 discrete image tokens, so the count is 8192·512 = 4,194,304. The FFN first maps from 512 to 2048, requiring 512·2048 = 1,048,576 weights, then maps from 2048 to 512, requiring 2048·512 = 1,048,576 weights. Total FFN weights are 2,097,152. If biases were included, the additional parameters would be 2048+512, but the provided marking scheme counts only matrix weights.
explanation: This is direct matrix parameter counting: rows times columns for each learned linear weight matrix.

statement: Question 5. 1. The Perceptron training loop updates w ← w + y_i x_i whenever y_i <w,x_i> ≤ 0. If w is initialized to 0, show that w can be written as w=Σ_i α_i y_i x_i and explain α_i. 2. Show how to evaluate sgn(<w,x>) using α_i and inner products <x,x_i>, and hence how to kernelize Perceptron using κ(x,z)=<φ(x),φ(z)>. 3. Given a normalized kernel κ and modified kernel κ~(x,z)=κ(x,z)+aδ(x,z), a>0, with distinct training examples, show there exists α such that K~α=y. Hence argue the training set is separable in the feature space of κ~. 4. Give an upper bound on the number of kernel Perceptron updates using κ~ in terms of α.
answer: 1. α_i starts at 0 and counts how many times example i caused an update, so w=Σ_i α_i y_i x_i. 2. sgn(<w,x>)=sgn(Σ_i α_i y_i <x_i,x>), and in feature space this becomes sgn(Σ_i α_i y_i κ(x_i,x)). 3. K~=K+aI is positive definite because K is positive semidefinite and a>0, so it is nonsingular and α=K~^{-1}y exists. With w=Σ_i α_i φ~(x_i), the training outputs satisfy K~α=y, giving a separating representation. 4. A Perceptron update bound is R^2/γ^2=(1+a)α^T K~ α=(1+a)y^Tα=(1+a)y^T K~^{-1}y≤m(1+a)/a.
solution: Initially w=0, so all α_i=0. Every update on example i adds y_i x_i to w; equivalently increment α_i by 1. By induction after any number of updates w=Σ_i α_i y_i x_i. For a test point x, <w,x>=<Σ_i α_i y_i x_i,x>=Σ_i α_i y_i <x_i,x>, so the classifier is sgn(Σ_i α_i y_i <x_i,x>). Replacing x by φ(x) gives sgn(Σ_i α_i y_i <φ(x_i),φ(x)>)=sgn(Σ_i α_i y_i κ(x_i,x)), requiring only kernel evaluations. For the modified kernel, the Gram matrix is K~=K+aI. Since K is positive semidefinite and aI is strictly positive definite for a>0, K~ is positive definite and invertible. Therefore α=K~^{-1}y exists. Taking w=Σ_i α_i φ~(x_i), the vector of training inner products equals K~α=y, so each labeled training point is correctly separated in the modified feature space. For the bound, the margin of the normalized separating vector is γ=1/||w||=1/sqrt(α^T K~α). The radius is R=sqrt(κ~(x,x))=sqrt(1+a). Novikoff's Perceptron bound gives R^2/γ^2=(1+a)α^T K~α=(1+a)y^Tα=(1+a)y^T K~^{-1}y. Since K~ has diagonal at least a beyond a PSD matrix, the supplied bound is ≤m(1+a)/a.
explanation: The problem shows the dual view of Perceptron and why adding a positive diagonal term to a normalized kernel can make distinct training examples separable.

statement: Question 6. A 3×3 grid world has states s1..s9 arranged as rows [s1 s2 s3], [s4 s5 s6], [s7 s8 s9]. Actions are up, down, left, right; attempts outside the grid leave the agent in the same state. Rewards: R(s1, attempt right)=1, R(s2, attempt down)=2, all others 0. Transitions are stochastic: with probability 0.7 the agent moves in the chosen direction, with probability 0.1 it moves left, 0.1 right, and 0.1 down. Start at s1 and γ=0.9. 1. With V initialized to 0, calculate Q(s1,right) after attempting right in the first iteration. 2. Derive the Bellman equation for s1 under policy π that chooses attempt right in s1 and attempt down in all other states. 3. Compute Vπ for policy π.
answer: 1. Q(s1,right)=1. 2. V(s1)=1+0.9(0.8V(s2)+0.1V(s1)+0.1V(s4)). 3. Under the supplied solution, only s1,s2,s3 have nonzero values: V(s1)=2.904191735, V(s2)=2.281686776, V(s3)=0.225661329, and V(s4)=...=V(s9)=0.
solution: 1. Q(s1,right)=R(s1,right)+γΣ_s'P(s'|s1,right)V(s'). From s1, attempting right reaches s2 with probability 0.7 plus the stochastic 'right' probability 0.1, stays in s1 with probability 0.1 from stochastic left, and reaches s4 with probability 0.1 from stochastic down. Thus Q(s1,right)=1+0.9(0.8V(s2)+0.1V(s1)+0.1V(s4)). With all V initialized to 0, Q=1. 2. Since π chooses right in s1, the Bellman equation is V(s1)=R(s1,right)+γ(0.8V(s2)+0.1V(s1)+0.1V(s4))=1+0.9(0.8V(s2)+0.1V(s1)+0.1V(s4)). 3. Following the provided answer key, values below the top row are zero because rewards are only accessible from the top row under the policy abstraction used. The simultaneous equations are V(s1)=1+0.9(0.1V(s1)+0.8V(s2)), V(s2)=2+0.9(0.1V(s1)+0.1V(s3)), and V(s3)=0.9(0.1V(s3)+0.1V(s2)). In matrix form: [[0.91,-0.72,0],[-0.09,1,-0.09],[0,-0.09,0.91]][V(s1),V(s2),V(s3)]^T=[1,2,0]^T. Solving gives V(s1)=2.904191735, V(s2)=2.281686776, and V(s3)=0.225661329. Specifically, eliminating V(s3) gives [[0.91,-0.72],[-0.0819,0.9019]][V(s1),V(s2)]^T=[1,1.82]^T, then V(s3)=0.09V(s2)/0.91.
